Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Let $0\le\beta<1$ and put $\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}>0$
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). Define
$\Lambda_\beta:V\to V$ by $(\Lambda_\beta v)^0=\gamma(v^0-\beta v^1)$,
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^1=\gamma(v^1-\beta v^0)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)^2=v^2$,
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^3=v^3$. Then $\Lambda_\beta$ is linear
([[def-linear-map]]), $\Lambda_\beta$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map,
and more precisely: (a) $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$ for
all $v,w\in V$; (b) $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; (c) $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$;
(d) $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$. In particular a future causal vector
has future causal image and $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=\eta(v,v)$
for every $v$ ([[def-real-order]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]]). The hypothesis
$0\le\beta<1$ is not removable: at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with time orientation
$C^+$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] is the form;
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] fixes $C^+$), and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with spatial three-space $S$ and
Euclidean form $\delta$. Then:

(i) For every $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and for every unit spatial
vector $e\in S$ and all $\beta_1,\beta_2\in(-1,1)$ one has
$B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$;
in particular collinear boosts commute. For each fixed unit spatial axis $e$
and scalar $b\in(-1,1)$ the collinear boost $B(be)$ satisfies $b=\tanh(r)$
for a unique scalar **rapidity** $r\in\mathbb R$, and rapidities add for
boosts along that same fixed axis. This signed scalar rapidity statement does
not identify a vector $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with the scalar
$\tanh(r)$.

(ii) $SO^+(V,\eta)$ is a subgroup of $O(V,\eta)$, which is a subgroup of the
general linear group $GL(V)$; every passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
every spatial rotation of the frame belongs to
$SO^+(V,\eta)$.

(iii) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ has a unique factorization
$L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and $\widehat R$
the extension of a spatial rotation of the frame; here
$\boldsymbol\beta=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ where $(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$ are the
coordinates of $u=Le_0$. Consequently every proper orthochronous Lorentz map
is the product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation, in that order, and
$L$ is itself a passive boost if and only if the rotation $\widehat R$ is the
identity.

(iv) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ preserves the interval $\eta(v,v)$, the causal
classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the
orientation, and the oriented volume form of the model:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,Lv_1,Lv_2,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]). An arbitrary
element $L$ of $O(V,\eta)$ satisfies $\det L=\pm1$ and either preserves or
interchanges the future and past cones; moreover $\det L=1$ alone does not
force $L(C^+)=C^+$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space, let $x$ and $x'$ be
inertial charts whose transition is the affine map $x'(p)=\Lambda x(p)+b$ with
linear part $\Lambda$ (a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix by
[[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]), and let
$\Omega\subseteq A$ be an open subset. Fix $\ell\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$ and $r,s\in\mathbb N$. Let $J:\Omega\to V$, $k:\Omega\to V^*$ and $T:\Omega\to T^{r,s}(V)$ be a
$\mathcal C^\ell$ vector field, a $\mathcal C^\ell$ covector field and a
$\mathcal C^\ell$ type-$(r,s)$ tensor field on $\Omega$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], with components $J^a$, $k_a$ and
$T^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}$ in the chart $x$, and primed components in
the chart $x'$. Use indices $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, summing every repeated upper/lower index. All component identities compare the same event $p$; as coordinate functions their arguments are $u=x(p)$ and $u\prime=x\prime(p)=\Lambda u+b$. Then:

(i) $J'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bJ^b$: a contravariant index gains the factor
$\Lambda^a{}_b$, that is, components transform by multiplication with the
transition matrix;

(ii) $k'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ak_b$: a covariant index gains the factor
$(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a$. If $\theta(p)=k_ax^a(p)+\theta_0$ is an affine scalar
function with constant covector $k$ and constant $\theta_0$, then
$\theta(p)=k'_ax'^a(p)+\theta'_0$ with $k'$ as above and
$\theta'_0:=\theta_0-k'_ab^a$, so the phase function is invariant when the
constant term is transformed together with the covector;

(iii) $T'^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}
=\Lambda^{a_1}{}_{c_1}\cdots\Lambda^{a_r}{}_{c_r}
(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_1}{}_{b_1}\cdots(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_s}{}_{b_s}
T^{c_1\dots c_r}{}_{d_1\dots d_s}$: every contravariant index gains a factor
$\Lambda$ and every covariant index a factor $\Lambda^{-1}$, and the law is
consistent with the multilinear evaluation of $T(p)$ after substituting the
transformed basis. Every contraction of one contravariant with one covariant
index is invariant, and the metric components satisfy
$\eta'_{ab}=\eta_{ab}$;

(iv) the coordinate partial-derivative operators satisfy
$\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a\partial_b$ when applied to scalar functions
at points where their coordinate representations are totally differentiable.
Consequently, at every event where the component functions of $J$ are totally
differentiable, the divergence is invariant,
$\partial'_aJ'^a=\partial_aJ^a$. These total differentials exist at every
event if $\ell\ge1$; for $\ell=0$ this clause applies only at events where the
specified components are totally differentiable, and does not assert
covariance from the existence of separate partial derivatives alone. For a
$\mathcal C^1$ type-$(2,0)$ field $T$ one has
$\partial'_aT'^{ab}=\Lambda^b{}_c\partial_aT^{ac}$;

(v) alternating covariant tensor fields transform by the covariant law on each
slot; the oriented volume form of the model satisfies
$\epsilon'_{abcd}=\epsilon_{abcd}$, since $\det\Lambda=+1$, whereas a general
Lorentz matrix with $\det=-1$ changes its sign;

(vi) let $J$ be a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field with components
$(J^0,J^1,J^2,J^3)$ in an inertial chart, and write the spatial block as
$J_{\mathrm{cov}}:=(J^1,J^2,J^3)$ and denote by $\partial_i$ the spatial
partial derivatives in the chart. Then the continuity equation
$\partial_aJ^a=0$ is equivalent to
$\partial_0J^0+\sum_i\partial_iJ^i=0$, and under the passive boost with
parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$ ($\Lambda=B(\boldsymbol\beta)$,
$\Lambda^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$) the components transform as
$J'^0=\gamma(J^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})$ and
$J'_{\mathrm{cov}}=J_{\mathrm{cov}}
+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})\boldsymbol\beta
-\gamma\boldsymbol\beta J^0$;

(vii) if $U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ future timelike vector field and $\rho_0$ a
$\mathcal C^1$ scalar field, then $J:=\rho_0U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field
and its first component is $J^0=\rho_0U^0$. Future timelikeness gives $U^0>0$
in every inertial chart, so one may define the normalized chart direction
$u:=U/U^0$ and the coordinate density $\rho:=J^0$. Then $u^0=1$,
$u^i=U^i/U^0$, $\rho=\rho_0U^0$, and $J=\rho u$ pointwise. The coordinate
density $\rho$ and scalar multiplier $\rho_0$ are different objects:
$\rho=\rho_0$ if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-1)=0$; at points where
$\rho_0\neq0$ equality holds exactly when $U^0=1$. The vector $u$ is a
normalized chart direction; it is not assumed to have unit or four-velocity
normalization. In an $x^0=ct$ convention the associated spatial coordinate
velocity, if interpreted as such, has components $cu^i$; physical
current/density identification requires its own model premise.

**Interpretation boundary.** The identification of a physical charge-current
with a vector field, and of $\rho$ with a measured charge density, is a model
premise of the electromagnetic framework; this item is a statement about the
transformation of components of specified fields and does not by itself assert
that any physical current transforms as a vector.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

The condition $\det L=1\ne0$ makes $L$ invertible by
[[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]. Fix $p_0\in A$; then
$F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ by the affine condition, and the map
$r\mapsto p_0+L^{-1}(r-F(p_0))$ is its inverse, so $F$ is a bijection.

For clarity, the induced transformation of tensors has the following precise
meaning. The **algebraic dual** $V^*$ is the vector space of linear maps
$\alpha:V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).
For integers $r,s\ge0$, a **type $(r,s)$ tensor** is a map
$T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$ linear in each argument; write
$\mathcal T^r_s(V)$ for their vector space with pointwise operations
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]). A **tensor
field** here is an assignment $T:A\to\mathcal T^r_s(V)$; each particular
model specifies its tensor types, domains and required regularity. Its
transformed field is defined by

$$(F_*T)_{F(p)}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r,w_1,\ldots,w_s):=T_p(\alpha_1\circ L,\ldots,\alpha_r\circ L,L^{-1}w_1,\ldots,L^{-1}w_s).$$

This is well defined since $F$ is bijective and all slot maps are linear;
for a restricted domain $D\subseteq A$ the new domain is $F(D)$. In particular
scalar fields transform by composition with $F^{-1}$ and vector fields by
$v_p\mapsto Lv_p$ at $F(p)$, since $\alpha(Lv_p)=(\alpha\circ L)(v_p)$.

Adopt the assumption that every solution configuration of each specified
mechanical or electromagnetic model is carried to a solution of that same
model by relabelling events with $F$ and applying the displayed transformations
to its fields and displacements. This is the meaning of **covariance** here;
which equations and admissible configurations constitute a model is specified
when that model is introduced.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with time orientation
$C^+$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] is the form;
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] fixes $C^+$), and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with spatial three-space $S$ and
Euclidean form $\delta$. Then:

(i) For every $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and for every unit spatial
vector $e\in S$ and all $\beta_1,\beta_2\in(-1,1)$ one has
$B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$;
in particular collinear boosts commute. For each fixed unit spatial axis $e$
and scalar $b\in(-1,1)$ the collinear boost $B(be)$ satisfies $b=\tanh(r)$
for a unique scalar **rapidity** $r\in\mathbb R$, and rapidities add for
boosts along that same fixed axis. This signed scalar rapidity statement does
not identify a vector $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with the scalar
$\tanh(r)$.

(ii) $SO^+(V,\eta)$ is a subgroup of $O(V,\eta)$, which is a subgroup of the
general linear group $GL(V)$; every passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
every spatial rotation of the frame belongs to
$SO^+(V,\eta)$.

(iii) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ has a unique factorization
$L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and $\widehat R$
the extension of a spatial rotation of the frame; here
$\boldsymbol\beta=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ where $(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$ are the
coordinates of $u=Le_0$. Consequently every proper orthochronous Lorentz map
is the product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation, in that order, and
$L$ is itself a passive boost if and only if the rotation $\widehat R$ is the
identity.

(iv) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ preserves the interval $\eta(v,v)$, the causal
classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the
orientation, and the oriented volume form of the model:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,Lv_1,Lv_2,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]). An arbitrary
element $L$ of $O(V,\eta)$ satisfies $\det L=\pm1$ and either preserves or
interchanges the future and past cones; moreover $\det L=1$ alone does not
force $L(C^+)=C^+$.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be its spatial three-space with
$\delta$ the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Then $\delta$ is a
positive-definite symmetric bilinear form, $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is
$\delta$-orthonormal, and $S=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\}$.

A **spatial rotation of the frame** is a linear map $R:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) such that

1. $R(e_0)=e_0$;
2. $R(S)\subseteq S$, so that the restriction $R|_S$ is an endomorphism of
   $S$;
3. $\delta(Rw,Rz)=\delta(w,z)$ for all $w,z\in S$; and
4. the restriction $R|_S$ has determinant $+1$ computed in the ordered basis
   $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]).

Condition 3 makes $R|_S$ injective, since $Rw=0$ with $w\in S$ forces
$\delta(w,w)=\delta(Rw,Rw)=0$ and hence $w=0$ by positive definiteness;
$S$ being finite-dimensional, $R|_S$ is then an automorphism of $S$, so in
fact $R(S)=S$. The extension of such an $R|_S$ by $R(e_0)=e_0$ is also
written $R$ and called a spatial rotation of the frame.

**Matrix form and the group $SO(3)$.** Via the $\delta$-orthonormal basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, a linear map of $V$ fixing $e_0$ and preserving $S$
corresponds to the block matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,A)$ with
$A\in M_3(\mathbb R)$; under this correspondence the maps of conditions 1-4
are exactly those with

$$A^{T}A=I_3\qquad\text{and}\qquad\det A=+1 .$$

Indeed, the matrix of the adjoint of an endomorphism of the inner product
space $(S,\delta)$ in a $\delta$-orthonormal basis is the transpose of its
matrix ([[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]]), and an
endomorphism of a finite-dimensional inner product space preserves the inner
product exactly when $T^{*}T=I$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-isometry-characterisations]],
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]). Writing
$SO(3):=\{A\in M_3(\mathbb R):A^{T}A=I_3,\ \det A=+1\}$, the orthogonal
operators on $S$ form a group and each of them has determinant $\pm1$
([[cor-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators-form-groups-and-have-unit-determinant-modulus]]),
and $\det(S_1S_2)=\det(S_1)\det(S_2)$ for composable endomorphisms
([[thm-operator-determinant-is-multiplicative]]); hence the determinant-one
part is a subgroup, the spatial rotations of the frame form a subgroup of the
general linear group of $V$, that is, of the group of invertible linear maps
$V\to V$ under composition
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]), and the map
$R\mapsto A(R)$ sending a rotation to
the matrix of $R|_S$ in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is a group isomorphism onto
$SO(3)$. The determinant in condition 4 is taken with respect to the
orientation of $S$ induced by the ordered basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ fixed by the
frame, so a change of frame changes which maps are called spatial rotations.
No claim is made here that spatial rotations are Lorentz maps; that is proved
in [[lem-boost-rotation-factorization]].

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,
$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over
a field $F$ ([[def-dimension]]).

If $\dim V=n\geq 1$, choose an ordered basis $\mathcal B$ and define

$$\det(T):=\det([T]_{\mathcal B}),$$

where $[T]_{\mathcal B}$ is the coordinate matrix of $T$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]) and the determinant on
the right is the matrix determinant
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]). If $V=\{0\}$, define $\det(T):=1$.

The positive-dimensional definition is justified by
[[thm-operator-determinant-is-basis-independent]], which proves that the value
does not depend on the chosen ordered basis.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ with its inertial chart $x$,
the electric and magnetic fields $E,B$ of [[def-em-fields]], the source fields
$(\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]] and the SI conventions of
[[def-em-si-conventions]] with $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be those of the
framework. Let $F$ be the electromagnetic two-form of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] with the components fixed there,
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, $F^{0i}=E_i/c$,
$F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let $j=(c\rho,J)$ carry the
tensor-component identification adopted in [[def-em-sources]]. Write
$\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t$ and $\partial_i$ for the coordinate partial
derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and
$\operatorname{div},\operatorname{curl}$ for those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Assume the smooth branch of
the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]: $E,B$ are jointly
$C^1$ on $\Omega\times I$ with the additional derivatives required by each
displayed equation existing and continuous, and $\rho,J$ are continuous. Then:

(a) [Equivalence] On $I\times\Omega$ the four smooth-branch equations

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

hold if and only if the two systems

$$(\mathrm{TM1})\quad \partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=-\mu_0\,j^\nu\quad(\nu=0,1,2,3),$$

$$(\mathrm{TM2})\quad \partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0\quad(\lambda,\mu,\nu\in\{0,1,2,3\})$$

hold on $I\times\Omega$. Every instance of (TM2) with a repeated index vanishes
identically because $F$ is alternating, so (TM1) and (TM2) carry exactly eight
independent scalar equations: (TM1) with $\nu=0$ is
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ (using $\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0=1$),
(TM1) with $\nu=i$ is the $i$-th component of
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, (TM2) with
$(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=(1,2,3)$ is $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and the three cyclic
triples $(0,i,j)$ are the three components of
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$; conversely these eight scalar equations
reproduce the two systems.

(b) [Form invariance under a change of inertial description] Let $x'$ be another
inertial chart with transition $x'=\Lambda x+b$, $\Lambda$ a proper
orthochronous Lorentz matrix (the changes of inertial description adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]), and let the primed components of the same
objects be the tensor components of [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]
(iii): $F'^{\,ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$,
$F'_{ab}=(\Lambda^{-1})^c{}_a(\Lambda^{-1})^d{}_bF_{cd}$,
$j'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bj^b$. Then (TM1) holds in $x$ if and only if (TM1) holds in
$x'$ with $j'$, and (TM2) holds in $x$ if and only if it holds in $x'$; by (a)
applied in both charts the four smooth-branch equations are likewise
form-invariant, the primed fields satisfying the primed equations with the
primed sources.

(c) [Hypotheses actually used] Only first derivatives of $E,B$ occur; the
equivalence uses exactly the component dictionary, the alternating character of
$F$, the constants $\mu_0,c,\varepsilon_0$ and the identification
$j=(c\rho,J)$, and the covariance clause uses the constant-coefficient
component law and the invertibility of $\Lambda$. No potential, no second
derivative, no boundary, decay or smoothness hypothesis beyond the stated
class, and no converse from the wave equations to the Maxwell equations is used
or asserted.

(d) [Scope] Only the smooth branch is covered; the weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and field or source points of singular support are
excluded. The conventions $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ fix the
signs of (TM1), and the alternative sign convention, which reverses the form of
the sourced equation, is not mixed with them. The statement is conditional on
the adopted postulates, uses no choice principle and makes no empirical claim.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

derivations.claim: (Clause (a): the axis boost components) For a spatial vector $W$ write $W_\parallel:=(W\cdot e_1)e_1$ and $W_\perp:=W-W_\parallel$. By [F2] and [F3](iii), $F'^{ab}=\Lambda_\beta{}^a{}_c\Lambda_\beta{}^b{}_dF^{cd}$ on the overlap; substituting the nonzero entries of [F2] and the components of [F1] gives $F'^{01}=\Lambda^0{}_0\Lambda^1{}_1F^{01}+\Lambda^0{}_1\Lambda^1{}_0F^{10}=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)F^{01}=F^{01}$, $F'^{02}=\Lambda^0{}_0\Lambda^2{}_2F^{02}+\Lambda^0{}_1\Lambda^2{}_2F^{12}=\gamma(E_2/c-\beta B_3)$, $F'^{03}=\gamma(E_3/c+\beta B_2)$, $F'^{12}=\Lambda^1{}_0\Lambda^2{}_2F^{02}+\Lambda^1{}_1\Lambda^2{}_2F^{12}=\gamma(B_3-\beta E_2/c)$, $F'^{13}=-\gamma(B_2+\beta E_3/c)$ and $F'^{23}=F^{23}=B_1$, because $F^{00}=F^{11}=0$, $F^{10}=-E_1/c$, $F^{02}=E_2/c$, $F^{03}=E_3/c$, $F^{12}=B_3$, $F^{13}=-B_2$ and $F^{23}=B_1$ by [F1]. Reading the dictionary [F1] in the primed chart, $E'_i=cF'^{0i}$ and $F'^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B'_k$, gives $E'_1=E_1$, $E'_2=\gamma(E_2-\beta cB_3)$, $E'_3=\gamma(E_3+\beta cB_2)$, $B'_1=B_1$, $B'_2=\gamma(B_2+\beta E_3/c)$ and $B'_3=\gamma(B_3-\beta E_2/c)$. Since $v=\beta ce_1$, the coordinate formulas of [F6] give $v\times B=\beta c\,(0,-B_3,B_2)$ and $v\times E=\beta c\,(0,-E_3,E_2)$; hence $(E+v\times B)_\perp=(0,E_2-\beta cB_3,E_3+\beta cB_2)$ and $(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp=(0,B_2+\beta E_3/c,B_3-\beta E_2/c)$, so the transverse formulas and the unchanged parallel components read $E'_\parallel=E_\parallel$, $B'_\parallel=B_\parallel$, $E'_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and $B'_\perp=\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$, as claimed.

(Clause (c), rotation case; the orientation identity) Let $A\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ satisfy $A^{\mathsf T}A=I_3$ and $\det A=+1$, and let $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(1,A)$; then the components $F'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$ of [F3] satisfy $E'=AE$ and $B'=AB$. First $F'^{0i}=A^i{}_jF^{0j}$, so $E'_i=cF'^{0i}=A^i{}_jE_j$. For the magnetic block, the dictionary gives $B'_q=\tfrac12\epsilon_{qij}F'^{ij}$, since inserting $F'^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijp}B'_p$ yields $\tfrac12\epsilon_{qij}\epsilon_{ijp}B'_p=\delta_{qp}B'_p$ by the elementary contraction $\epsilon_{qij}\epsilon_{ijp}=2\delta_{qp}$ (direct enumeration of the two contributing index pairs). Hence $B'_q=\tfrac12\epsilon_{qij}A^i{}_kA^j{}_l\epsilon_{klm}B_m$, and the matrix $A$ satisfies the cofactor identity $\epsilon_{qij}A^i{}_kA^j{}_l=A^q{}_m\epsilon_{mkl}$ for all $q,k,l$: the determinant of the matrix with columns $(c_m,c_k,c_l)$ of $A$ equals $\epsilon_{mkl}\det A=\epsilon_{mkl}$ by column alternation [F7], and it also equals $\sum_{n,i,j}\epsilon_{nij}A^n{}_mA^i{}_kA^j{}_l$ by the permutation expansion [F7]; multiplying that equality by $A^q{}_m$ and summing over $m$ turns the factor $A^q{}_mA^n{}_m$ into $(AA^{\mathsf T})^{qn}=\delta^{qn}$ and yields the identity, where $AA^{\mathsf T}=I_3$ holds because $A^{\mathsf T}A=I_3$ with $\det A=1\ne0$ makes $A$ invertible with inverse $A^{\mathsf T}$ [F7]. Then $B'_q=\tfrac12A^q{}_m\epsilon_{mkl}\epsilon_{klp}B_p=A^q{}_m\delta_{mp}B_p=A^q{}_mB_m$ by the elementary identity $\epsilon_{mkl}\epsilon_{klp}=2\delta_{mp}$ (direct enumeration), so $B'=AB$. If $A$ is the matrix in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of a spatial rotation $R$ of the frame, then $A^{\mathsf T}A=I_3$ and $\det A=+1$ by [F5], and $E'=RE$, $B'=RB$, which is the rotation case of clause (c).

(Conjugation of the vector boost) Let $v\in\mathbb R^3$ with $0<|v|<c$, put $u:=v/|v|$ and $\beta:=|v|/c\in(0,1)$, so $v/c=\beta u$. Among the standard basis vectors $e_1,e_2,e_3$ at most one is a multiple of $u$ (two independent vectors cannot both be nonzero multiples of one vector), so let $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ be the least index for which $e_j$ is not a multiple of $u$; set $\hat a:=\bigl(e_j-(e_j\cdot u)u\bigr)/\lVert e_j-(e_j\cdot u)u\rVert_2$, whose denominator is nonzero because $e_j$ is not a multiple of $u$, and $b:=u\times\hat a$. Then $(u,\hat a,b)$ is an orthonormal family, since $u\cdot\hat a=0$, $\lVert u\rVert_2=\lVert\hat a\rVert_2=1$, $b$ is orthogonal to $u$ and $\hat a$, and $\lVert b\rVert_2^2=\lVert u\rVert_2^2\lVert\hat a\rVert_2^2-(u\cdot\hat a)^2=1$ [F6]; it is positively oriented because $\det[u\ \hat a\ b]=\langle u\times\hat a,b\rangle=\lVert b\rVert_2^2=1$ [F6]. Let $S$ be the matrix with columns $u,\hat a,b$ and $R:=S^{\mathsf T}$, so the rows of $R$ are $u,\hat a,b$ and $Ru=e_1$; then $S^{\mathsf T}S=I_3$, $\det S=1$ and, since $\det S=1\ne0$, $S$ is invertible with $S^{-1}=S^{\mathsf T}$, so $SS^{\mathsf T}=I_3$, $R^{-1}=R^{\mathsf T}$ and $\det R=\det(S^{\mathsf T})=\det S=1$ [F7]. The conjugation identity $\widehat RB(v/c)\widehat R^{-1}=\Lambda_\beta$, where $\widehat R:=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$, follows by direct substitution in the matrix of [F2]: for all $x\in V$ set $y:=\widehat Rx$, so $y^0=x^0$, $y_{\mathrm{vec}}=Rx_{\mathrm{vec}}$ and $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=R^{\mathsf T}y_{\mathrm{vec}}$; since $u\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}=u\cdot R^{\mathsf T}y_{\mathrm{vec}}=(Ru)\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=y^1_{\mathrm{vec}}$ and $(v/c)\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}=\beta y^1_{\mathrm{vec}}$, the formula of [F2] with parameter $\beta u$ gives $(\widehat RB(v/c)x)^0=(B(v/c)x)^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta u\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})=\gamma(y^0-\beta y^1_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and $(\widehat RB(v/c)x)_{\mathrm{vec}}=R\bigl(R^{\mathsf T}y_{\mathrm{vec}}+(\gamma-1)y^1_{\mathrm{vec}}u-\gamma\beta y^0u\bigr)=y_{\mathrm{vec}}+(\gamma-1)y^1_{\mathrm{vec}}e_1-\gamma\beta y^0e_1$ using $(Ru)=e_1$; with $\widehat Rx=y$ this is exactly $\Lambda_\beta y$ by the matrix of [F2]. Hence $B(v/c)=\widehat R^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_\beta\widehat R$.

(Regularity of the primed components) The overlap $V=U\cap U'$ is open and carries both charts: $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $x'(U')$ are open in $\mathbb R^4$, the affine map $x\mapsto\Lambda^{-1}(x-b)$ carries $x'(U')$ bijectively onto $x(U')$, and $x$ carries $V$ onto the open set $x(U)\cap x(U')$ because $x$ and $x'$ are bijections [F3, F4]. On $V$ the primed component functions $F'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$ and $j'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bj^b$ are constant-coefficient finite linear combinations of the unprimed component functions [F3], so $E',B'$ inherit the joint class of $E,B$ under the fixed linear relabelling of the dictionary [F1], the additional derivatives required by each displayed equation exist and are continuous, and $\rho',J'$ are continuous whenever $\rho,J$ are.

(Clause (a′): arbitrary-direction boost) Let $v\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|v|<c$. If $v=0$, then $B(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$ [F2], the charts differ by the translation $x'=x+b$, the components are unchanged by [F3], so $E'=E$ and $B'=B$, and the closed formulas reduce to the identity because $\gamma_v=1$ and all terms carrying $v$ vanish; no parallel direction is needed. Let $v\ne0$ and use $u,\hat a,b,S,R,\beta$ and the conjugation identity $B(v/c)=\widehat R^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_\beta\widehat R=\operatorname{diag}(1,S)\Lambda_\beta\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ of step 1.3. By [F3] the total component law of the composite is the matrix product of the factors of $B(v/c)=\widehat R^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_\beta\widehat R$; applied successively, the first stage is the rotation $\widehat R=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ (step 1.2 with $A=R$, whose hypotheses $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$ hold by step 1.3), giving $E''=RE$, $B''=RB$; the second stage is the axis boost $\Lambda_\beta$ in the intermediate frame, where step 1.1 applies because its proof uses only the dictionary and the component law; the third stage is the rotation $\widehat R^{\mathsf T}=\operatorname{diag}(1,R^{\mathsf T})$ (step 1.2 with $A=R^{\mathsf T}$, whose hypotheses $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_3$ and $\det(R^{\mathsf T})=\det R=1$ hold by step 1.3 and [F7]), giving $E'=R^{\mathsf T}E'''$ and $B'=R^{\mathsf T}B'''$. Writing $\parallel,\perp$ for the components along $e_1$ in the intermediate coordinates, step 1.1 applied in the intermediate frame gives $E'''=E''_\parallel+\gamma(E''+\beta c\,e_1\times B'')_\perp$ and $B'''=B''_\parallel+\gamma(B''-\beta c\,e_1\times E''/c^2)_\perp$; applying $S=R^{\mathsf T}$ to the intermediate vectors and using the cross-product identity $R^{\mathsf T}(p\times q)=(R^{\mathsf T}p)\times(R^{\mathsf T}q)$ for the orthogonal matrix $R$ (obtained from the identity of step 1.2 by applying $R$ to both sides: $R\bigl((R^{\mathsf T}p)\times(R^{\mathsf T}q)\bigr)=(RR^{\mathsf T}p)\times(RR^{\mathsf T}q)=p\times q$) gives $R^{\mathsf T}(E''+\beta ce_1\times B'')=E+\beta c\,(R^{\mathsf T}e_1)\times(R^{\mathsf T}B'')=E+v\times B$, since $R^{\mathsf T}e_1=S e_1=u$ and $v=\beta cu$; moreover $R^{\mathsf T}E''_\parallel=(e_1\cdot E'')R^{\mathsf T}e_1=(u\cdot E)u=E_\parallel$ and $R^{\mathsf T}B''_\parallel=(u\cdot B)u=B_\parallel$. Hence $E'=E_\parallel+\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and $B'=B_\parallel+\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$, which is the stated parallel/perpendicular form, and it yields $E'_\parallel=E_\parallel$, $B'_\parallel=B_\parallel$ by taking inner products with $u$. Finally $E_\parallel+\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)-(\gamma-1)(u\cdot E)u$ and $(\gamma-1)(u\cdot E)u=\frac{\gamma^2}{\gamma+1}\frac{v(v\cdot E)}{c^2}$, because $(u\cdot E)u=(v\cdot E)v/|v|^2$ and $(\gamma-1)/\beta^2=\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)$ [F2]; the same computation for $B$ gives the displayed closed formulas for every $v\ne0$, with $\gamma_v=\gamma$ since $|v|/c=\beta$.

(Clause (b): the invariants under the axis boost) Substituting the components of step 1.1, $|B'|^2-\frac{|E'|^2}{c^2}=B_1^2-\frac{E_1^2}{c^2}+\gamma^2\bigl[(B_2+\beta E_3/c)^2+(B_3-\beta E_2/c)^2\bigr]-\frac{\gamma^2}{c^2}\bigl[(E_2-\beta cB_3)^2+(E_3+\beta cB_2)^2\bigr]$; the linear terms cancel in pairs and the transverse contributions combine to $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)\bigl(B_2^2+B_3^2-(E_2^2+E_3^2)/c^2\bigr)=B_2^2+B_3^2-(E_2^2+E_3^2)/c^2$ because $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ [F2], giving the first display. Likewise $E'\cdot B'=E_1B_1+\gamma^2\bigl[(E_2-\beta cB_3)(B_2+\beta E_3/c)+(E_3+\beta cB_2)(B_3-\beta E_2/c)\bigr]=E_1B_1+\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)(E_2B_2+E_3B_3)=E\cdot B$, since the mixed terms cancel in pairs. By [F1] the scalar fields $I_1$ and $I_2$ computed from the components in $x$ are $|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$ and $4E\cdot B/c$, and those computed from the components in $x'$ are the same expressions in the primed fields, so the two displays say exactly that $I_1$ and $I_2$ take the same values in the two charts.

(Clause (c): general proper orthochronous changes) Let $\Lambda$ be proper orthochronous with chart $x'=\Lambda x+b$. By [F3] the primed components are $F'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$, which is the first assertion. By [F4] there is a unique $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and a spatial rotation $R$ of the frame with $\Lambda=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$. Taking the intermediate chart $x''=\widehat Rx$ and the final chart $x'=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)x''+b$ realizes the same transition $x'=\Lambda x+b$; by step 1.2 the intermediate fields are $E''=RE$, $B''=RB$, and by step 2.1 applied with velocity $v=-c\boldsymbol\beta$ — for which $|v|=c|\boldsymbol\beta|<c$ and $B(v/c)=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ [F2] — the final fields are $E'=E''_\parallel+\gamma_v(E''+v\times B'')_\perp$ and $B'=B''_\parallel+\gamma_v(B''-v\times E''/c^2)_\perp$, with $\gamma_v=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$. This is exactly the statement that the change acts first by $(E,B)\mapsto(RE,RB)$ and then by the boost law (a′) with velocity $-c\boldsymbol\beta$; the axis-only law of (a) was not substituted for it.

(Clause (b), general changes: the two scalar combinations) Every proper orthochronous change preserves $|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$ and $E\cdot B$. Indeed, writing $\Lambda=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ by [F4], the transformation factorizes into the rotation $\widehat R$, the axis boost $\Lambda_\beta$ in the intermediate frame and the inverse rotation, as in step 2.1; a spatial rotation with matrix $A$ satisfying $A^{\mathsf T}A=I_3$ preserves the Euclidean norm and inner product of vectors, $|AE|^2=|E|^2$, $|AB|^2=|B|^2$ and $(AE)\cdot(AB)=E\cdot B$ [F5]; and the axis boost preserves the two combinations $|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$ and $E\cdot B$ by step 2.2. Chaining the three stages gives the invariance for every proper orthochronous change, hence in particular for the boost chart $x'$ of clause (b), and by [F1] the equivalently stated invariance of $I_1$ and $I_2$.

(Clause (d): form invariance of the smooth Maxwell branch) Let $x'=\Lambda x+b$ with $\Lambda$ proper orthochronous, and assume that on $V$ the four smooth-branch equations of [F9] hold for $(E,B,\rho,J)$. By [F8] the two tensor systems $(\mathrm{TM1})$ and $(\mathrm{TM2})$ hold in $x$ on $V$ and therefore also hold in $x'$ on $V$ with the primed components of the same $F$ and the same four-current, and then the four smooth-branch equations hold in $x'$ for the primed dictionary fields; the primed fields are exactly the fields $E',B'$ read in the dictionary [F1], which by step 3.1 are the components of the same $F$ given by the component law, and the primed sources are $(c\rho',J')$ because $j'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bj^b$ with $j^0=c\rho$, $j^i=J^i$ [F3, F1]. The hypotheses of [F8] in the chart $x'$ are met because the primed fields and sources are again of the required class on the open set $V$ by step 1.4. The converse is the same chain with the roles of $x$ and $x'$ exchanged, since $\Lambda^{-1}$ is again a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix [F4].

(Hypotheses and scope) Clause (a) is step 1.1, clause (a′) is step 2.1, clause (b) is steps 2.2 and 3.2, clause (c) is steps 1.2 and 3.1, and clause (d) is step 4.1. The argument used only the component dictionary and invariants [F1], the two boost matrices and the identity $(\gamma-1)/\beta^2=\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)$ [F2], the constant component law and the invertibility of the changes of chart [F3, F4], the unique factorization of a proper orthochronous Lorentz map [F4], the matrix form and determinant of a spatial rotation [F5], the cross-product and Euclidean identities [F6], the determinant identities [F7], the tensor equivalence of [F8] and the smooth Maxwell branch [F9]. Only finitely many choices are made (the least index $j$ in step 1.3 and the finite index sets of [F7]); no choice principle, no potential, no derivative of the fields beyond the class required by the cited statements, no boundary, decay or medium hypothesis and no empirical premise are used. All clauses are pointwise on the open overlap of the two chart restrictions and conditional on the adopted postulates; orientation-reversing changes are outside the framework's conventions [F1], and no apparatus, detector or measurement model is introduced.

boundaries.reason: Every clause is a pointwise component formula or scalar identity on the open chart overlap; no finite set, family or union is quantified over.

boundaries.evidence: The zero-boost case v=0 is an exact case in step 2.1 (B(0)=id_V, E'=E, B'=B and the closed formulas reduce to the identity), and zero fields satisfy every displayed component and invariant identity trivially.
The neutral change is the case A=I_3 of step 1.2 (A^T A=I_3 and det A=+1 hold trivially) composed with v=0 in step 2.1, leaving the components unchanged.

The degenerate lightlike limit |v|=c is excluded by the hypotheses |v|<c used in step 2.1 and 0<|v|<c in step 1.3; orientation-reversing changes (det A=-1) are outside the det A=+1 hypothesis of step 1.2, as recorded in the Statement scope and step 5.1.

boundaries.reason: The formulas are pointwise algebraic identities on the open overlap analysed in step 1.4; the v=0 case is a separate exact case in step 2.1, not an endpoint limit, and no boundary or asymptotic values are taken.

Step 4.1 states and proves the converse by exchanging the roles of x and x' (Lambda inverse proper orthochronous), so both directions of the form-invariance biconditional are established.
