Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be the oriented Lorentz vector space of the affine Minkowski model with orientation and volume form $\varepsilon$ of [[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], and let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be an alternating bilinear form ([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]], [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Define the Hodge dual by $(*F)_{ab}:=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ and set $(\alpha\wedge\beta)_{ab}:=\alpha_a\beta_b-\alpha_b\beta_a$. Use the standard form normalization $F=\tfrac12\sum_{a,b}F_{ab}\theta^a\wedge\theta^b$ in the dual coframe $\theta^a(e_b)=\delta^a_b$ of an oriented orthonormal frame, and define $(F\wedge F)(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3):=2[F(v_0,v_1)F(v_2,v_3)-F(v_0,v_2)F(v_1,v_3)+F(v_0,v_3)F(v_1,v_2)]$, the alternating four-form exterior square. Let $n\in V$ be future unit, $\eta(n,n)=-1$, and put $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$. (a) $e(n)=b(n)=0$, and $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$ with $n^\flat:=\eta(n,\cdot)$; also $*(*F)=-F$, so the Hodge dual squares to $-1$ on two-forms. (b) In an oriented orthonormal frame with $n=e_0$: $e_i=F_{i0}$, $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$, $F_{0i}=-e_i$ and $F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$; hence the six components of $F$ are exactly the six components of the pair $(e,b)$ and the reconstruction in (a) is equivalent to these component formulae. (c) The quadratic invariants are $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|b|^2-|e|^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=-4\,(e\cdot b)$, where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are those of the spatial structure of the frame ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]); also $F\wedge F=2(e\cdot b)\varepsilon$. The two scalar expressions $I_1:=\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}$ and $I_2:=F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}$ form a basis of the homogeneous quadratic polynomials in the six components of $F$ invariant under the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; the square-wedge expression is dependent, $F\wedge F=-\tfrac12 I_2\varepsilon$. $I_2$ is an oriented pseudoscalar and changes sign if the chosen orientation is reversed with the metric and $F$ held fixed. (d) (Optional SI identification.) Let $c>0$. If in an inertial frame one identifies $F^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ for numerical spatial vectors $E,B\in\mathbb R^3$, then $e_i=-E_i/c$ and $b_i=B_i$, the invariants of (c) read $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=4\,(E\cdot B)/c$, and $F\wedge F=-2(E\cdot B)\varepsilon/c$. If $\kappa:=(F\wedge F)(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(F\wedge F)_{0123}$, then $E\cdot B=-c\kappa/2$. Under the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] along $e_1$ with parameter $\beta\in(-1,1)$ one has $E'_1=E_1$, $B'_1=B_1$, $E'_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and $B'_\perp=\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$ where the cross product is the right-handed product ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), with $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ and $v=\beta c$ along $e_1$. In an SI reading, $c$ has units $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, $E$ has units $\mathrm V/\mathrm m$ and $B$ has units tesla, so $E/c$ and all components of $F$ have units tesla; these are conditional unit assignments, not measurements. (e) The theorem is algebra on the oriented Lorentz vector space with the stated index and duality conventions; clause (d) is an explicitly optional identification of the components of $F$ with fields the electromagnetic framework names $E,B$, and the theorem asserts no field equation, no dynamics, no measurement and no transformation beyond the stated component law. No choice principle is used.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with time orientation
$C^+$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] is the form;
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] fixes $C^+$), and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with spatial three-space $S$ and
Euclidean form $\delta$. Then:

(i) For every $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and for every unit spatial
vector $e\in S$ and all $\beta_1,\beta_2\in(-1,1)$ one has
$B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$;
in particular collinear boosts commute. For each fixed unit spatial axis $e$
and scalar $b\in(-1,1)$ the collinear boost $B(be)$ satisfies $b=\tanh(r)$
for a unique scalar **rapidity** $r\in\mathbb R$, and rapidities add for
boosts along that same fixed axis. This signed scalar rapidity statement does
not identify a vector $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with the scalar
$\tanh(r)$.

(ii) $SO^+(V,\eta)$ is a subgroup of $O(V,\eta)$, which is a subgroup of the
general linear group $GL(V)$; every passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
every spatial rotation of the frame belongs to
$SO^+(V,\eta)$.

(iii) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ has a unique factorization
$L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and $\widehat R$
the extension of a spatial rotation of the frame; here
$\boldsymbol\beta=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ where $(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$ are the
coordinates of $u=Le_0$. Consequently every proper orthochronous Lorentz map
is the product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation, in that order, and
$L$ is itself a passive boost if and only if the rotation $\widehat R$ is the
identity.

(iv) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ preserves the interval $\eta(v,v)$, the causal
classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the
orientation, and the oriented volume form of the model:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,Lv_1,Lv_2,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]). An arbitrary
element $L$ of $O(V,\eta)$ satisfies $\det L=\pm1$ and either preserves or
interchanges the future and past cones; moreover $\det L=1$ alone does not
force $L(C^+)=C^+$.

Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^k$ fields of [[def-em-fields]] on the laboratory region
$U\cong I\times\Omega$ of an inertial chart $x$ of the framework
([[def-em-lab-geometry]]), $k\ge1$, with the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $F$ be the electromagnetic two-form of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] with its fixed components
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, $F^{0i}=E_i/c$,
$F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Let $0\le\beta<1$, $\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$,
$v:=\beta c\,e_1$, and let $\Lambda_\beta$ be the explicit boost of
[[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]] with
$\Lambda_\beta{}^0{}_0=\Lambda_\beta{}^1{}_1=\gamma$,
$\Lambda_\beta{}^0{}_1=\Lambda_\beta{}^1{}_0=-\gamma\beta$,
$\Lambda_\beta{}^2{}_2=\Lambda_\beta{}^3{}_3=1$ and all other entries zero. Let
$x'=\Lambda_\beta x+b$ be the corresponding inertial chart, and for every event
$p$ in the overlap of the two chart restrictions define the primed field
components by reading the components of the same $F$ in $x'$ through the
dictionary of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], so that $F'_{0i}=-E'_i/c$,
$F'_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B'_k$ at $p$. Then:

(a) [Boosted fields] at every such $p$, with $\parallel$ and $\perp$ the
components along and orthogonal to $e_1$ in the spatial Euclidean structure of
the chart,
$$E'_1=E_1,\quad B'_1=B_1,\qquad E'_\parallel=E_\parallel,\quad B'_\parallel=B_\parallel,\qquad E'_\perp=\gamma\,(E+v\times B)_\perp,\qquad B'_\perp=\gamma\,(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp,$$
equivalently, componentwise,
$E'_2=\gamma(E_2-\beta cB_3)$, $E'_3=\gamma(E_3+\beta cB_2)$,
$B'_2=\gamma(B_2+\beta E_3/c)$, $B'_3=\gamma(B_3-\beta E_2/c)$.

(a′) [Arbitrary boost direction] For a velocity vector $v\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$|v|<c$, use the actual vector boost $B(v/c)$ of [[def-lorentz-boost]], with
$\gamma_v=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. If $v\ne0$, decompose the fields along
$\widehat v=v/|v|$ and its orthogonal complement. Then $E'_\parallel=E_\parallel$,
$B'_\parallel=B_\parallel$, $E'_\perp=\gamma_v(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and
$B'_\perp=\gamma_v(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$. Equivalently, for every $v$,
including $v=0$,
$$E'=\gamma_v(E+v\times B)-\frac{\gamma_v^2}{\gamma_v+1}\frac{v(v\cdot E)}{c^2},\qquad B'=\gamma_v(B-v\times E/c^2)-\frac{\gamma_v^2}{\gamma_v+1}\frac{v(v\cdot B)}{c^2}.$$
At $v=0$ these are the identity and no preferred parallel direction is
assigned.

(b) [Invariants] at every such $p$,
$$|B'|^2-\frac{|E'|^2}{c^2}=|B|^2-\frac{|E|^2}{c^2},\qquad E'\cdot B'=E\cdot B;$$
equivalently the scalar fields $I_1:=\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$
and $I_2:=F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=4\,E\cdot B/c$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]
(b) take the same values whether computed from the components in $x$ or in
$x'$.

(c) [General proper orthochronous changes] for any proper orthochronous Lorentz
matrix $\Lambda$ with chart $x'=\Lambda x+b$, the primed components of $F$ are
given by the component law of [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] (iii),
$F'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$; in particular, if
$\Lambda=\widehat R$ is the extension of a spatial rotation $R$ of the frame
([[def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame]]), then $E'=RE$ and $B'=RB$, and
by the unique factorization $\Lambda=B(-\beta)\widehat R$ of
[[thm-sr-proper-orthochronous-lorentz-algebra]] (iii) every proper
orthochronous change acts first by $(E,B)\mapsto(RE,RB)$ and then by the
arbitrary-direction boost law (a′) with velocity $-c\beta$, where $\beta$ is
the vector parameter of that factorization. The axis-only law (a) is not
substituted for a general vector boost.

(d) [Form invariance of the Maxwell branch] if $(E,B,\rho,J)$ satisfy the
smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] in $x$ on the overlap, and
$(\rho',J')$ are the components of the same four-current in $x'$, then
$(E',B',\rho',J')$ satisfy the same four equations in $x'$, by
[[pthm-em-tensor-maxwell-equivalence]].

(e) [Scope] All clauses are pointwise on the overlap $U\cap U'$ of the two
chart restrictions, are conditional on the adopted postulates, and concern the
smooth classical flat branch; no accelerating coordinates, curved spacetime,
material medium, apparatus or empirical claim is involved; the transformation
is exact algebra, and the primed component functions are $C^k$ wherever the
overlap is open. The invariants clause uses only the proper orthochronous
changes of description adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]];
orientation-reversing changes are outside the framework's field conventions
([[def-em-fields]]).

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

The condition $\det L=1\ne0$ makes $L$ invertible by
[[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]. Fix $p_0\in A$; then
$F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ by the affine condition, and the map
$r\mapsto p_0+L^{-1}(r-F(p_0))$ is its inverse, so $F$ is a bijection.

For clarity, the induced transformation of tensors has the following precise
meaning. The **algebraic dual** $V^*$ is the vector space of linear maps
$\alpha:V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).
For integers $r,s\ge0$, a **type $(r,s)$ tensor** is a map
$T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$ linear in each argument; write
$\mathcal T^r_s(V)$ for their vector space with pointwise operations
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]). A **tensor
field** here is an assignment $T:A\to\mathcal T^r_s(V)$; each particular
model specifies its tensor types, domains and required regularity. Its
transformed field is defined by

$$(F_*T)_{F(p)}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r,w_1,\ldots,w_s):=T_p(\alpha_1\circ L,\ldots,\alpha_r\circ L,L^{-1}w_1,\ldots,L^{-1}w_s).$$

This is well defined since $F$ is bijective and all slot maps are linear;
for a restricted domain $D\subseteq A$ the new domain is $F(D)$. In particular
scalar fields transform by composition with $F^{-1}$ and vector fields by
$v_p\mapsto Lv_p$ at $F(p)$, since $\alpha(Lv_p)=(\alpha\circ L)(v_p)$.

Adopt the assumption that every solution configuration of each specified
mechanical or electromagnetic model is carried to a solution of that same
model by relabelling events with $F$ and applying the displayed transformations
to its fields and displacements. This is the meaning of **covariance** here;
which equations and admissible configurations constitute a model is specified
when that model is introduced.

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework, extending [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] (ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines, with coordinate speed $c$ in every inertial chart) and [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] (the affine Minkowski model, with the model's equations covariant under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps):

**(i) Ideal plane wave.** An ideal monochromatic light wave in vacuum is modeled, in any inertial chart, by a dimensionless affine phase $\theta$ with future null wave covector $k$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]], [[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]]): the level sets of $\theta$ are the wave fronts, and the complete ray trajectories of this wave are the constant-phase lines $\lambda\mapsto p+\lambda k^\sharp$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, whose tangents are future null. Their future portions from $p$ have images $p+\mathbb R_{\ge0}k^\sharp$. The complete trajectories are ideal light rays in the sense of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]; the portions are half-lines. The model is one ideal plane wave: constant wave covector, no medium, no dispersion, no absorption, no modulation or envelope, no boundary or source model, no intensity or polarization model.

**(ii) Frequency reading.** An ideal observer of the model with four-velocity $U_o=cn$ ($n$ future unit timelike) that receives this wave reads the angular frequency $\omega_n:=-ck(n)=-k(U_o)$ and the linear frequency $\omega_n/(2\pi)$ of [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]], that is, minus the rate of change of the phase with respect to the observer's own proper time with the sign convention that this number is positive ([[lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline]], [[lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative]]). The reading is attached to the observer's worldline at the event of reception.

**(iii) Frequency comparisons.** Comparing the frequency of one wave between two ideal observers or between two inertial descriptions means comparing $\omega_n$ at specified reception events, or the frame data $(\omega,s)$ of the same phase function in specified inertial charts; this postulate asserts no Doppler or aberration formula, and comparing events requires propagating the phase along the specified observer worldlines.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** These are adopted idealizations, not deductions from experiment and not claims about nature. No quantum photon model and no identification of energy with $\hbar\omega$ is made; no claim is made that real light, real clocks, real receivers or real sources are exactly described; dispersive, absorbing, nonlinear or modulated media, finite line width, intensity, polarization, source and detector physics, gravitation, quantum effects and accelerated-observer reception are outside the model. Empirical tests of the model belong to the framework's experimental work and are not asserted here.

No choice principle is used in this formulation; the postulate is an adopted assumption of the model, not a proved assertion.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements, with the SI coordinate and unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and
$\gamma:I\to A$ a curve. Choose an inertial chart $\chi$ with
$E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$ as in [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Require
$y:=\chi\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R^4$ to be $C^1$ on the interior of $I$,
with its derivative extending continuously to any included endpoints, where
it is the one-sided derivative. Define the displacement-valued derivative by
$\dot\gamma(s):=E(y'(s))\in V$ and require $\dot\gamma(s)\in C^+$ everywhere,
including such endpoints. This derivative is chart-independent: a second
chart has coordinates $\widetilde y=M^{-1}(y-\chi(o'))$, so its
parameter derivative is $M^{-1}\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$, while its basis map
is $E'=EM$; their product is $E\,\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$.

An **ideal clock on this curve** has a reading map $\sigma:I\to\mathbb R$
in seconds, specified up to an additive constant, with, for all $a<b$ in $I$,

$$\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(\dot\gamma(s),\dot\gamma(s)\bigr)}\,\mathrm ds .$$

The integrand is positive and continuous on $[a,b]$: the coordinate derivatives
are continuous, $\eta$ is a finite bilinear expression, and the square root
is continuous at every positive argument, as follows from
$|\sqrt r-\sqrt q|=|r-q|/(\sqrt r+\sqrt q)$ for $r,q>0$.
Thus [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] applies to this compact interval
and gives a well-defined Riemann integral. The reading rule contains no
additional acceleration-dependent correction (**clock hypothesis**); it does
not require $C^2$ regularity or an acceleration to exist. This is an adopted
physical interpretation of the length integral, not a proof about real clocks.

**(ii) Ideal light.** In vacuum, the **ideal light rays** are the oriented
straight lines parametrized by $\ell:\mathbb R\to A$,
$\ell(\lambda)=p+\lambda v$, where $p\in A$ and $v\in V$ is future null;
increasing $\lambda$ specifies their future direction. In an inertial chart
$\chi$ their coordinate map is

$$\chi(\ell(\lambda))=\chi(p)+\lambda\,(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3).$$

Since the chart's time-axis vector is future, the cone description of
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] gives
$v^0=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert>0$. With $t=\chi^0/c$ the spatial
coordinate velocity is $c(v^1,v^2,v^3)/v^0$ and has Euclidean magnitude $c$
in every inertial chart. The conversion constant is the same across charts;
its exact SI numerical value is a unit convention as specified in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], while the ideal-vacuum-light
interpretation is an adopted, empirically testable model assumption.

Adopt [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]], [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and [[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]], and the conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $x$ and $x'$ be inertial charts whose transition is $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ with $\beta\in\mathbb R^3$, $|\beta|<1$, $b\in\mathbb R^4$ and $B(\beta)$ the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]]; write $\gamma:=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}:=\beta/|\beta|$ for $\beta\ne0$, so that the frame $x'$ moves with velocity $v=c\beta$ relative to the frame $x$ in the direction $\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ (step 1.1 records this). Let the ideal wave of the model have phase $\theta$ with future null wave covector $k$ and frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$ in the sense of [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]: $\omega>0$, $s\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|s|=1$ and $k_a=(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3)$ in $x$. Then, conditionally on the adopted model:

**(i) Frame data in $x'$.** The data of the same covector $k$ in $x'$ is $(\omega',s')$ with

$$\omega'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\,\omega>0,\qquad s'=\frac{s+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)\beta-\gamma\beta}{\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)}$$

for $\beta\ne0$ (and $\omega'=\omega$, $s'=s$ for $\beta=0$), so $|s'|=1$ and $k'_a=(-\omega'/c,(\omega'/c)s'_1,(\omega'/c)s'_2,(\omega'/c)s'_3)$ in $x'$. In the axis case $\beta=be_1$ with $b\in(-1,1)$: $s'_1=(s_1-b)/(1-bs_1)$ and $(s'_2,s'_3)=(s_2,s_3)/[\gamma(1-bs_1)]$.

**(ii) Reading and frequency ratios.** The rest observers of $x$ and $x'$ (four-velocities $ce_0$ and $ce'_0$) read angular frequencies $\omega=-ck(e_0)$ and $\omega'=-ck(e'_0)$; the linear frequencies and wavelengths of the two descriptions satisfy $\nu'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\nu$ and $\lambda'=\lambda/[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)]$. More generally, an ideal inertial observer whose constant coordinate velocity in $x$ is $w$ (a vector of the frame's spatial three-space with $|w|<c$) reads

$$\omega_o=\gamma_w\Bigl(1-\frac{w\cdot s}{c}\Bigr)\omega,\qquad \gamma_w:=\Bigl(1-\frac{|w|^2}{c^2}\Bigr)^{-1/2};$$

equivalently $\omega_o=\gamma_w(1-\beta_w\cdot s)\omega$ with $\beta_w:=w/c$.

**(iii) Longitudinal cases.** For $\beta\ne0$, if $s=\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ then $\omega'=\omega\sqrt{(1-|\beta|)/(1+|\beta|)}<\omega$, $\nu'=\nu\sqrt{(1-|\beta|)/(1+|\beta|)}$ and $\lambda'=\lambda\sqrt{(1+|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|)}$: the observer moving in the direction of propagation (in the interpretation of a source at rest in $x$ located behind the observer) reads a red-shifted frequency and lengthened wavelength. If $s=-\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ then $\omega'=\omega\sqrt{(1+|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|)}>\omega$ and $\lambda'=\lambda\sqrt{(1-|\beta|)/(1+|\beta|)}$: blue shift for an observer moving opposite to the propagation direction (toward such a source). At $\beta=0$ every direction has $\omega'=\omega$, $\nu'=\nu$ and $\lambda'=\lambda$; no normalized boost axis is defined.

**(iv) Transverse protocols.** If $\beta\cdot s=0$ (propagation direction perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame $x$) then $\omega'=\gamma\omega$; this is greater than $\omega$ when $\beta\ne0$ and equals $\omega$ when $\beta=0$. If $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$, equivalently $s'\cdot\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}=0$ for $\beta\ne0$ (propagation direction perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame $x'$), then $\omega'=\omega/\gamma$; this is less than $\omega$ when $\beta\ne0$ and equals $\omega$ when $\beta=0$. Both configurations are called transverse Doppler configurations in the literature, and the two factors differ for $\beta\ne0$: the direction and size of the shift are not determined by the word "transverse" without specifying the frame in which transversality holds.

**(v) Aberration.** For $\beta\ne0$, define $\theta_x:=\arccos(\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}\cdot s)$ and $\theta_{x'}:=\arccos(\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}\cdot s')$ in $[0,\pi]$, using the angular convention of [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]. The primed scalar product uses the same numerical axis components in the primed frame's spatial coordinates; the two rest spaces themselves are distinct. Then

$$\cos\theta_{x'}=\frac{\cos\theta_x-|\beta|}{1-|\beta|\cos\theta_x};$$

the map $u\mapsto(u-|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|u)$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $[-1,1]$ onto itself, and in particular $\cos\theta_x=0$ gives $\cos\theta_{x'}=-|\beta|$.

**(vi) Scope and protocol.** All clauses concern one ideal plane wave and ideal observers, and frequencies are compared through the phase model at specified reception events; the results are conditional on the adopted postulates (ideal plane wave, ideal clocks, inertial covariance, flat classical spacetime) and are not empirical claims about nature, sources or apparatus. They exclude media and dispersion, modulation and signal speeds, intensity and polarization, real line widths, accelerating observers, gravitation and quantum effects; no statistical or measurement statement is made. If $\beta=0$ the transition is the pure translation $x'=x+b$: the inertial axes and wave-covector frame data agree, with $\omega'=\omega$ and $s'=s$, while the affine phase constant is transformed as in the covector and phase law.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space, let $x$ and $x'$ be
inertial charts whose transition is the affine map $x'(p)=\Lambda x(p)+b$ with
linear part $\Lambda$ (a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix by
[[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]), and let
$\Omega\subseteq A$ be an open subset. Fix $\ell\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$ and $r,s\in\mathbb N$. Let $J:\Omega\to V$, $k:\Omega\to V^*$ and $T:\Omega\to T^{r,s}(V)$ be a
$\mathcal C^\ell$ vector field, a $\mathcal C^\ell$ covector field and a
$\mathcal C^\ell$ type-$(r,s)$ tensor field on $\Omega$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], with components $J^a$, $k_a$ and
$T^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}$ in the chart $x$, and primed components in
the chart $x'$. Use indices $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, summing every repeated upper/lower index. All component identities compare the same event $p$; as coordinate functions their arguments are $u=x(p)$ and $u\prime=x\prime(p)=\Lambda u+b$. Then:

(i) $J'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bJ^b$: a contravariant index gains the factor
$\Lambda^a{}_b$, that is, components transform by multiplication with the
transition matrix;

(ii) $k'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ak_b$: a covariant index gains the factor
$(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a$. If $\theta(p)=k_ax^a(p)+\theta_0$ is an affine scalar
function with constant covector $k$ and constant $\theta_0$, then
$\theta(p)=k'_ax'^a(p)+\theta'_0$ with $k'$ as above and
$\theta'_0:=\theta_0-k'_ab^a$, so the phase function is invariant when the
constant term is transformed together with the covector;

(iii) $T'^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}
=\Lambda^{a_1}{}_{c_1}\cdots\Lambda^{a_r}{}_{c_r}
(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_1}{}_{b_1}\cdots(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_s}{}_{b_s}
T^{c_1\dots c_r}{}_{d_1\dots d_s}$: every contravariant index gains a factor
$\Lambda$ and every covariant index a factor $\Lambda^{-1}$, and the law is
consistent with the multilinear evaluation of $T(p)$ after substituting the
transformed basis. Every contraction of one contravariant with one covariant
index is invariant, and the metric components satisfy
$\eta'_{ab}=\eta_{ab}$;

(iv) the coordinate partial-derivative operators satisfy
$\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a\partial_b$ when applied to scalar functions
at points where their coordinate representations are totally differentiable.
Consequently, at every event where the component functions of $J$ are totally
differentiable, the divergence is invariant,
$\partial'_aJ'^a=\partial_aJ^a$. These total differentials exist at every
event if $\ell\ge1$; for $\ell=0$ this clause applies only at events where the
specified components are totally differentiable, and does not assert
covariance from the existence of separate partial derivatives alone. For a
$\mathcal C^1$ type-$(2,0)$ field $T$ one has
$\partial'_aT'^{ab}=\Lambda^b{}_c\partial_aT^{ac}$;

(v) alternating covariant tensor fields transform by the covariant law on each
slot; the oriented volume form of the model satisfies
$\epsilon'_{abcd}=\epsilon_{abcd}$, since $\det\Lambda=+1$, whereas a general
Lorentz matrix with $\det=-1$ changes its sign;

(vi) let $J$ be a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field with components
$(J^0,J^1,J^2,J^3)$ in an inertial chart, and write the spatial block as
$J_{\mathrm{cov}}:=(J^1,J^2,J^3)$ and denote by $\partial_i$ the spatial
partial derivatives in the chart. Then the continuity equation
$\partial_aJ^a=0$ is equivalent to
$\partial_0J^0+\sum_i\partial_iJ^i=0$, and under the passive boost with
parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$ ($\Lambda=B(\boldsymbol\beta)$,
$\Lambda^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$) the components transform as
$J'^0=\gamma(J^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})$ and
$J'_{\mathrm{cov}}=J_{\mathrm{cov}}
+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})\boldsymbol\beta
-\gamma\boldsymbol\beta J^0$;

(vii) if $U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ future timelike vector field and $\rho_0$ a
$\mathcal C^1$ scalar field, then $J:=\rho_0U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field
and its first component is $J^0=\rho_0U^0$. Future timelikeness gives $U^0>0$
in every inertial chart, so one may define the normalized chart direction
$u:=U/U^0$ and the coordinate density $\rho:=J^0$. Then $u^0=1$,
$u^i=U^i/U^0$, $\rho=\rho_0U^0$, and $J=\rho u$ pointwise. The coordinate
density $\rho$ and scalar multiplier $\rho_0$ are different objects:
$\rho=\rho_0$ if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-1)=0$; at points where
$\rho_0\neq0$ equality holds exactly when $U^0=1$. The vector $u$ is a
normalized chart direction; it is not assumed to have unit or four-velocity
normalization. In an $x^0=ct$ convention the associated spatial coordinate
velocity, if interpreted as such, has components $cu^i$; physical
current/density identification requires its own model premise.

**Interpretation boundary.** The identification of a physical charge-current
with a vector field, and of $\rho$ with a measured charge density, is a model
premise of the electromagnetic framework; this item is a statement about the
transformation of components of specified fields and does not by itself assert
that any physical current transforms as a vector.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

The condition $\det L=1\ne0$ makes $L$ invertible by
[[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]. Fix $p_0\in A$; then
$F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ by the affine condition, and the map
$r\mapsto p_0+L^{-1}(r-F(p_0))$ is its inverse, so $F$ is a bijection.

For clarity, the induced transformation of tensors has the following precise
meaning. The **algebraic dual** $V^*$ is the vector space of linear maps
$\alpha:V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).
For integers $r,s\ge0$, a **type $(r,s)$ tensor** is a map
$T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$ linear in each argument; write
$\mathcal T^r_s(V)$ for their vector space with pointwise operations
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]). A **tensor
field** here is an assignment $T:A\to\mathcal T^r_s(V)$; each particular
model specifies its tensor types, domains and required regularity. Its
transformed field is defined by

$$(F_*T)_{F(p)}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r,w_1,\ldots,w_s):=T_p(\alpha_1\circ L,\ldots,\alpha_r\circ L,L^{-1}w_1,\ldots,L^{-1}w_s).$$

This is well defined since $F$ is bijective and all slot maps are linear;
for a restricted domain $D\subseteq A$ the new domain is $F(D)$. In particular
scalar fields transform by composition with $F^{-1}$ and vector fields by
$v_p\mapsto Lv_p$ at $F(p)$, since $\alpha(Lv_p)=(\alpha\circ L)(v_p)$.

Adopt the assumption that every solution configuration of each specified
mechanical or electromagnetic model is carried to a solution of that same
model by relabelling events with $F$ and applying the displayed transformations
to its fields and displacements. This is the meaning of **covariance** here;
which equations and admissible configurations constitute a model is specified
when that model is introduced.
