Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with time orientation
$C^+$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] is the form;
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] fixes $C^+$), and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with spatial three-space $S$ and
Euclidean form $\delta$. Then:

(i) For every $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and for every unit spatial
vector $e\in S$ and all $\beta_1,\beta_2\in(-1,1)$ one has
$B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$;
in particular collinear boosts commute. For each fixed unit spatial axis $e$
and scalar $b\in(-1,1)$ the collinear boost $B(be)$ satisfies $b=\tanh(r)$
for a unique scalar **rapidity** $r\in\mathbb R$, and rapidities add for
boosts along that same fixed axis. This signed scalar rapidity statement does
not identify a vector $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with the scalar
$\tanh(r)$.

(ii) $SO^+(V,\eta)$ is a subgroup of $O(V,\eta)$, which is a subgroup of the
general linear group $GL(V)$; every passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
every spatial rotation of the frame belongs to
$SO^+(V,\eta)$.

(iii) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ has a unique factorization
$L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and $\widehat R$
the extension of a spatial rotation of the frame; here
$\boldsymbol\beta=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ where $(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$ are the
coordinates of $u=Le_0$. Consequently every proper orthochronous Lorentz map
is the product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation, in that order, and
$L$ is itself a passive boost if and only if the rotation $\widehat R$ is the
identity.

(iv) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ preserves the interval $\eta(v,v)$, the causal
classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the
orientation, and the oriented volume form of the model:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,Lv_1,Lv_2,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]). An arbitrary
element $L$ of $O(V,\eta)$ satisfies $\det L=\pm1$ and either preserves or
interchanges the future and past cones; moreover $\det L=1$ alone does not
force $L(C^+)=C^+$.

Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^k$ fields of [[def-em-fields]] on the laboratory region
$U\cong I\times\Omega$ of an inertial chart $x$ of the framework
([[def-em-lab-geometry]]), $k\ge1$, with the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $F$ be the electromagnetic two-form of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] with its fixed components
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, $F^{0i}=E_i/c$,
$F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Let $0\le\beta<1$, $\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$,
$v:=\beta c\,e_1$, and let $\Lambda_\beta$ be the explicit boost of
[[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]] with
$\Lambda_\beta{}^0{}_0=\Lambda_\beta{}^1{}_1=\gamma$,
$\Lambda_\beta{}^0{}_1=\Lambda_\beta{}^1{}_0=-\gamma\beta$,
$\Lambda_\beta{}^2{}_2=\Lambda_\beta{}^3{}_3=1$ and all other entries zero. Let
$x'=\Lambda_\beta x+b$ be the corresponding inertial chart, and for every event
$p$ in the overlap of the two chart restrictions define the primed field
components by reading the components of the same $F$ in $x'$ through the
dictionary of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], so that $F'_{0i}=-E'_i/c$,
$F'_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B'_k$ at $p$. Then:

(a) [Boosted fields] at every such $p$, with $\parallel$ and $\perp$ the
components along and orthogonal to $e_1$ in the spatial Euclidean structure of
the chart,
$$E'_1=E_1,\quad B'_1=B_1,\qquad E'_\parallel=E_\parallel,\quad B'_\parallel=B_\parallel,\qquad E'_\perp=\gamma\,(E+v\times B)_\perp,\qquad B'_\perp=\gamma\,(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp,$$
equivalently, componentwise,
$E'_2=\gamma(E_2-\beta cB_3)$, $E'_3=\gamma(E_3+\beta cB_2)$,
$B'_2=\gamma(B_2+\beta E_3/c)$, $B'_3=\gamma(B_3-\beta E_2/c)$.

(a′) [Arbitrary boost direction] For a velocity vector $v\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$|v|<c$, use the actual vector boost $B(v/c)$ of [[def-lorentz-boost]], with
$\gamma_v=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. If $v\ne0$, decompose the fields along
$\widehat v=v/|v|$ and its orthogonal complement. Then $E'_\parallel=E_\parallel$,
$B'_\parallel=B_\parallel$, $E'_\perp=\gamma_v(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and
$B'_\perp=\gamma_v(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$. Equivalently, for every $v$,
including $v=0$,
$$E'=\gamma_v(E+v\times B)-\frac{\gamma_v^2}{\gamma_v+1}\frac{v(v\cdot E)}{c^2},\qquad B'=\gamma_v(B-v\times E/c^2)-\frac{\gamma_v^2}{\gamma_v+1}\frac{v(v\cdot B)}{c^2}.$$
At $v=0$ these are the identity and no preferred parallel direction is
assigned.

(b) [Invariants] at every such $p$,
$$|B'|^2-\frac{|E'|^2}{c^2}=|B|^2-\frac{|E|^2}{c^2},\qquad E'\cdot B'=E\cdot B;$$
equivalently the scalar fields $I_1:=\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$
and $I_2:=F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=4\,E\cdot B/c$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]
(b) take the same values whether computed from the components in $x$ or in
$x'$.

(c) [General proper orthochronous changes] for any proper orthochronous Lorentz
matrix $\Lambda$ with chart $x'=\Lambda x+b$, the primed components of $F$ are
given by the component law of [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] (iii),
$F'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$; in particular, if
$\Lambda=\widehat R$ is the extension of a spatial rotation $R$ of the frame
([[def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame]]), then $E'=RE$ and $B'=RB$, and
by the unique factorization $\Lambda=B(-\beta)\widehat R$ of
[[thm-sr-proper-orthochronous-lorentz-algebra]] (iii) every proper
orthochronous change acts first by $(E,B)\mapsto(RE,RB)$ and then by the
arbitrary-direction boost law (a′) with velocity $-c\beta$, where $\beta$ is
the vector parameter of that factorization. The axis-only law (a) is not
substituted for a general vector boost.

(d) [Form invariance of the Maxwell branch] if $(E,B,\rho,J)$ satisfy the
smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] in $x$ on the overlap, and
$(\rho',J')$ are the components of the same four-current in $x'$, then
$(E',B',\rho',J')$ satisfy the same four equations in $x'$, by
[[pthm-em-tensor-maxwell-equivalence]].

(e) [Scope] All clauses are pointwise on the overlap $U\cap U'$ of the two
chart restrictions, are conditional on the adopted postulates, and concern the
smooth classical flat branch; no accelerating coordinates, curved spacetime,
material medium, apparatus or empirical claim is involved; the transformation
is exact algebra, and the primed component functions are $C^k$ wherever the
overlap is open. The invariants clause uses only the proper orthochronous
changes of description adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]];
orientation-reversing changes are outside the framework's field conventions
([[def-em-fields]]).

derivations.claim: (Clause (a): laboratory components of $e$ and $b$) By [F2], $n^0=\gamma_w$ and $n^i=\gamma_w w_i/c$, so with the dictionary [F1] the covariant components are $e_0=F_{00}n^0+F_{0i}n^i=-(\gamma_w/c^2)E\cdot w$ and $e_i=F_{i0}n^0+F_{ij}n^j=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}E_i+\frac{\gamma_w}{c}\epsilon_{ijk}w_jB_k=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}\bigl(E_i+(w\times B)_i\bigr)$, using $F_{i0}=-F_{0i}=E_i/c$ and $(w\times B)_i=\epsilon_{ijk}w_jB_k$ [F1]. For the dual, the definition $(*F)_{ab}=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ and the components of [F1] give $(*F)_{0i}=B_i$ and $(*F)_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}E_k/c$: indeed $\varepsilon_{0i}{}^{jk}=\varepsilon_{0ijk}=\epsilon_{ijk}$ because raising the two spatial indices is free and $(0,i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(0,1,2,3)$ exactly when $(i,j,k)$ is even, so $(*F)_{0i}=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{jk\ell}B_\ell=B_i$ with $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{jk\ell}=2\delta_{i\ell}$ (direct enumeration); and $\varepsilon_{ij}{}^{0k}=\eta^{00}\eta^{kk}\varepsilon_{ij0k}=-\varepsilon_{ij0k}=-\epsilon_{ijk}$, since $(0,i,j,k)\mapsto(i,j,0,k)$ is an even permutation, so $(*F)_{ij}=\varepsilon_{ij}{}^{0k}F_{0k}=(-\epsilon_{ijk})(-E_k/c)=\epsilon_{ijk}E_k/c$. Hence $b_0=(*F)_{00}n^0+(*F)_{0i}n^i=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}B\cdot w$ and $b_i=(*F)_{i0}n^0+(*F)_{ij}n^j=-\gamma_wB_i+\frac{\gamma_w}{c^2}\epsilon_{ijk}w_jE_k=-\gamma_w\bigl(B_i-\frac{(w\times E)_i}{c^2}\bigr)$. These are the four displayed component formulas of clause (a); in particular the laboratory temporal components $e_0,b_0$ need not vanish, so the orthogonality of the decomposition cannot be read as the vanishing of these laboratory components.

(Clause (a): annihilation, raising, reconstruction) Since $F$ and $*F$ are alternating, $e(n)=F_{ab}n^an^b=0$ and $b(n)=(*F)_{ab}n^an^b=0$; equivalently $n^ae_a=n^ab_a=0$ [F1]. For the metric-dual vectors $e^\sharp,b^\sharp$, defined by $\eta(e^\sharp,v)=e(v)$ and $\eta(b^\sharp,v)=b(v)$ for all $v$, this gives $\eta(e^\sharp,n)=\eta(b^\sharp,n)=0$, so $e^\sharp,b^\sharp\in n^\perp$; since both covectors annihilate $n$, restricting them to $n^\perp$ and raising with the positive rest metric of [F2] gives the same vectors, and this is the raising used in the definitions $E_n=c\,e^\sharp$, $B_n=-b^\sharp$. By [F1] the reconstruction $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$ holds, and because the dictionary formulas of [F1] recover the six components of $F$ from $(e,b)$, the six rest components determine $F$ at the event. The measured vectors lie in the three-dimensional rest space $n^\perp$; they are not the laboratory coordinate triples $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$.

(Clause (a): the observer's inertial rest frame and the observed components) At $w=0$, $B(0)$ is the identity and $n=e_0$, so the rest frame is the laboratory frame and the displayed identity is immediate without a division by $|w/c|^2$. For $w\ne0$, applying the matrix of [F3] to the vector $n=\gamma_w(1,w/c)$ of [F2] gives $\bigl(B(w/c)n\bigr)^0=\gamma_w\bigl(\gamma_w-\frac{w}{c}\cdot\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}\bigr)=\gamma_w^2(1-|w|^2/c^2)=1$ and $\bigl(B(w/c)n\bigr)_{\mathrm{vec}}=\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}+\frac{\gamma_w-1}{|w/c|^2}\Bigl(\frac{w}{c}\cdot\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}\Bigr)\frac{w}{c}-\gamma_w\frac{w}{c}\gamma_w=\gamma_w\frac{w}{c}\bigl[1+(\gamma_w-1)-\gamma_w\bigr]=0$; hence $n$ has coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$ in the chart $x'=B(w/c)x+b$, that is $n=e'_0$: the chart $x'$ is the observer's inertial rest frame, and it is an admissible inertial change of description because $B(w/c)$ is proper orthochronous [F3]. By clause (a′) of [F3] the components of the same $F$ read in $x'$ are the boosted components with vector parameter $v=w$: $E'_\parallel=E_\parallel$, $B'_\parallel=B_\parallel$, $E'_\perp=\gamma_w(E+w\times B)_\perp$ and $B'_\perp=\gamma_w(B-w\times E/c^2)_\perp$ along $\widehat w$, with the displayed closed formulas, and $E'=E$, $B'=B$ when $w=0$. Reading the dictionary [F1] in the rest frame with $n=e'_0$ gives $e'_0=b'_0=0$, $e'_i=F'_{i0}=-F'_{0i}=E'_i/c$ and $b'_i=(*F')_{i0}=-(*F')_{0i}=-B'_i$; hence the vectors $E_n=c\,e^\sharp$ and $B_n=-b^\sharp$ have rest-frame components $(0,E')$ and $(0,B')$. Under the adopted model assumption [A1] the observed electric and magnetic fields in the rest frame are $E'$ and $B'$, that is: the components along $w$ are $E_\parallel$ and $B_\parallel$, the components perpendicular to $w$ are $\gamma_w(E+w\times B)_\perp$ and $\gamma_w(B-w\times E/c^2)_\perp$, and at $w=0$ the observer is the laboratory rest observer reading $E,B$ themselves with no distinguished direction of motion. The identification of the mathematical vectors with apparatus readings is exactly [A1] and is assumed, not proved.

(Clause (b): the phase covector, nonzero, future and null) By [F4] the wavevector is $\mathbf k=Ks$ with $|\mathbf k|=K=\omega/c$ and propagation direction $\widehat{\mathbf k}=s$, and the phase is $\theta(x,t)=\mathbf k\cdot x-\omega t$. Its coordinate derivative components are $k_0=\partial\theta/\partial x^0=c^{-1}\partial_t\theta=-\omega/c$ and $k_i=\partial\theta/\partial x^i=(\omega/c)s_i$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] with $x^0=ct$), so the phase covector is $k_a=(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3)$ and $\theta(p)=k_ax^a(p)$ up to an additive constant. Raising with $\eta$ gives $k^0=-k_0=\omega/c>0$ and $k_{\mathrm{vec}}=(k_1,k_2,k_3)=(\omega/c)s$, so $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=-(\omega/c)^2+(\omega/c)^2|s|^2=0$ and $k^\sharp\ne0$: the phase covector is nonzero, future ($k^0>0$) and null. By the amplitude equations of [F4] the fields are a source-free smooth Maxwell field on the whole-space region.

(Clause (b): exact frequency reading) At the reception event the ideal observer of [F5] with four-velocity $U_o=cn$ reads $\omega_n=-ck(n)=-k(U_o)$. With $k(n)=k_an^a=-\frac{\omega}{c}\gamma_w+\frac{\omega}{c}\frac{w\cdot s}{c}\gamma_w=-\frac{\omega}{c}\gamma_w\bigl(1-\frac{w\cdot s}{c}\bigr)$ from [F2] and step 1.4, this gives $\omega_n=\gamma_w\bigl(1-\frac{w\cdot s}{c}\bigr)\omega>0$, where the positivity is clause (ii) of [F6], whose formula this is with the frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$ of [F4] and the observer velocity $w$; its hypotheses hold by step 1.4 and the adopted model postulates [F5], [F6]. At $w=0$ one has $\gamma_w=1$ and $\omega_n=\omega$, and the reader is the laboratory rest observer of clause (a) reading $E,B$.

(Clause (b): aberration, longitudinal and transverse protocols) The data $(\omega,s)$ of [F4] are exactly the frame-$x$ data of the Doppler theorem [F6] for its future null wave covector (step 1.4), and the ideal plane-wave, ideal-clock and covariance postulates it adopts are those of the framework [F5], [F8]. Hence its clauses (i)-(v) apply verbatim to this wave: (i) in a chart $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ the frame data $(\omega',s')$ satisfy $\omega'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\omega>0$ with the displayed $s'$ satisfying $|s'|=1$ (the direction transformation, i.e. aberration); (iii) $s=\pm\widehat\beta$ give the longitudinal red- and blue-shift factors $\omega\sqrt{(1\mp|\beta|)/(1\pm|\beta|)}$ with the stated wavelength ratios; (iv) $\beta\cdot s=0$ gives $\omega'=\gamma\omega$ and $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$ gives $\omega'=\omega/\gamma$, the two transverse protocols, and the two factors differ when $\beta\ne0$; (v) the aberration relation $\cos\theta_{x'}=(\cos\theta_x-|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|\cos\theta_x)$ with the map a strictly increasing bijection of $[-1,1]$ onto itself and $\cos\theta_x=0\Rightarrow\cos\theta_{x'}=-|\beta|$. For $\beta=0$ clause (i) gives $\omega'=\omega$ and $s'=s$, so frequency and direction are unchanged and no aberration angle is defined; each formula carries its nonzero-motion qualification.

(Clause (b): composition of successive inertial changes) Let $x_1=\Lambda_1x_0+b_1$ and $x_2=\Lambda_2x_1+b_2$ be successive inertial changes with proper orthochronous $\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2$. The covector law [F7] gives $k_{1,a}=(\Lambda_1^{-1})^b{}_ak_{0,b}$ and $k_{2,a}=(\Lambda_2^{-1})^b{}_ak_{1,b}=((\Lambda_2\Lambda_1)^{-1})^b{}_ak_{0,b}$, with the affine phase constants transformed along with the translations. To compute the wave data for a general stage $x_j=\Lambda_jx_{j-1}+b_j$, factor $\Lambda_j=B(-\alpha_j)\widehat R_j$ with $|\alpha_j|<1$ and $\widehat R_j=\operatorname{diag}(1,R_j)$ a spatial rotation, by [F9]. The intermediate rotation leaves $k_0=-\omega_{j-1}/c$ unchanged and sends the spatial covector triple to $R_jk_{\mathrm{vec}}$, since $R_j^{-1}=R_j^{\mathsf T}$; hence it leaves the frequency unchanged and sends $s_{j-1}$ to $R_js_{j-1}$. Apply [F6] to the remaining boost with parameter $\beta_j=-\alpha_j$ and $\gamma_j:=(1-|\beta_j|^2)^{-1/2}$: $\omega_j=\gamma_j(1-\beta_j\cdot R_js_{j-1})\omega_{j-1}>0$, and $s_j$ is the aberration formula of [F6] applied to $R_js_{j-1}$. This includes zero boosts and pure rotations. Therefore $\omega_2/\omega_0=(\omega_2/\omega_1)(\omega_1/\omega_0)$, with the direction updated at every stage. This proves the composition claim for general inertial changes.

(Clause (c): status, scope and hypotheses) Clause (a) is steps 1.1-1.3: the four component formulas, the annihilation $e(n)=b(n)=0$, the raising into $n^\perp$, the reconstruction determining $F$ from $(e,b)$ and the identification of the observed rest-frame fields are established there, the last only under the adopted model assumption [A1]. Clause (b) is steps 1.4, 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3: the phase covector is nonzero, future and null; the frequency reading is $\omega_n=\gamma_w(1-w\cdot s/c)\omega>0$; the aberration, longitudinal and transverse conclusions are clauses (i)-(v) of [F6]; and successive inertial changes compose as stated. Clause (c) records that the split and reconstruction are pointwise for every future unit observer $n$, whereas the reading and aberration formulas were derived for an observer whose coordinate velocity is that of an inertial rest frame — an accelerating observer requires its own analysis, since no single rest frame exists and differentiating the decomposition adds derivatives of $n$ — and that the identification of $(E_n,B_n)$ and $\omega_n$ with apparatus readings is the adopted assumption [A1] together with the ideal-plane-wave and ideal-clock and ideal-light models [F5], [F8]. No calibration, apparatus, statistical or empirical claim is made, no photon model and no identification of frequency with energy by a factor $\hbar$ is used, and media, dispersion, modulation, boundaries and finite line widths are excluded. Only the dictionary [F1], the observer data [F2], the boost [F3], the plane-wave and Doppler data [F4], [F6], the reading rule [F5], the covector law [F7], the ideal clock and light assumptions [F8] and the adopted model assumption [A1] were used; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The clauses are pointwise statements at one event about one observer and one wave; no finite set, family or union is enumerated, so no empty case exists.

boundaries.evidence: The zero-velocity observer w=0 is exact in step 1.3 (E'=E, B'=B, no distinguished direction) and step 2.1 (gamma_w=1, omega_n=omega).

boundaries.reason: The observer vector n is unit in the general case (eta(n,n)=-1) and the wave data are a single fixed set; there is no family whose one-element case is a boundary subcase distinct from the general statement.

boundaries.evidence: Degeneracies are handled: the phase covector k is metric-degenerate (null) and nonzero with future time component in step 1.4, and the Beta=0 no-aberration case with undefined aberration angle is disposed of in step 2.2 with each formula carrying its nonzero-motion qualification.

Step 2.2 (v) records that the aberration map is a strictly increasing bijection of [-1,1] onto itself, so the endpoint directions cos(theta_x)=+-1 are included and mapped to +-1; no other boundary or limit is taken.

boundaries.reason: The observer rest frame and boosts are defined by explicit formulas and the wave data are given; step 4.1 records that no choice principle is used.

The clauses assert the identity F=n^flat wedge e - *(n^flat wedge b) with the six components determining F, and exact component and frequency formulas; no biconditional is asserted, so no forward iff case arises.

No biconditional is asserted: the reconstruction (e,b)->F is an explicit identity in step 1.2 and the reverse direction F->(e,b) is the definition e=F(.,n), b=(*F)(.,n) of step 1.1, neither an iff claim of the item.

derivations.claim: Source-free solution: the field pair $(E,B)$ is constant, hence $C^\infty$ with every first partial derivative continuous and equal to $0$, in particular jointly $C^k$ for every $k\ge1$ [F1]. With the divergence and curl of [F2], $\operatorname{div}E=\partial_1E_1+\partial_2E_2+\partial_3E_3=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=(\partial_2E_3-\partial_3E_2,\ \partial_3E_1-\partial_1E_3,\ \partial_1E_2-\partial_2E_1)=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$, and $\partial_tE=\partial_tB=0$; hence the four source-free smooth-branch equations of [F2] with $\rho=0$, $J=0$ hold on $\mathbb R^3…

Boosted components: substitute $E_1=0$, $E_2=E_0$, $E_3=0$ and $B_1=B_2=B_3=0$ in the formulas of [F3]: $E'_1=E_1=0$, $E'_2=\gamma(E_0-\beta c\cdot0)=\gamma E_0$, $E'_3=\gamma(0+\beta c\cdot0)=0$, $B'_1=B_1=0$, $B'_2=\gamma(0+\beta\cdot0/c)=0$ and $B'_3=\gamma(0-\beta E_0/c)=-\gamma\beta E_0/c$; therefore $E'=\gamma E_0e_2$ and $B'=-(\gamma\beta E_0/c)e_3=-(\gamma|v|E_0/c^2)e_3$, since $|v|=\beta c$ by $v=\beta ce_1$ and the right-handed basis [F1]. This is the asserted pair of components; the magnetic component is nonzero exactly when $\beta>0$, and the direction is $-e_3$.

Invariants: by [F3] the invariants agree with those computed from $(E,B)$, and directly from step 1.2, $|E'|^2=\gamma^2E_0^2$, $|B'|^2=\gamma^2\beta^2E_0^2/c^2$ and $E'\cdot B'=0$ by [F5] ($e_2\perp e_3$), while $|E|^2=E_0^2$, $|B|^2=0$ and $E\cdot B=0$; hence $|B'|^2-|E'|^2/c^2=\gamma^2E_0^2(\beta^2-1)/c^2=-E_0^2/c^2$ by $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ [F4], which equals $|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$, and $E'\cdot B'=0=E\cdot B$. At $\beta=0$ one has $\gamma=1$ and the formulas of [F3] give $E'=E$, $B'=B=0$, so the boosted description is the laboratory description and no magnetic field appears.

Closing: step 1.1 verifies that the constant data solve the source-free smooth branch; step 1.2 gives the exact boosted components and step 2.1 the two invariant checks, with the $\beta=0$ reduction. The computation is exact algebra for the constant field and uses only the dictionary and boost formulas of [F3]; no measurement, source model, finite-energy, boundary or empirical claim is made, and no choice principle is used.

The endpoint Beta=0 of the parameter interval [0,1) is treated exactly in step 2.1, reducing to the laboratory description; the other endpoint Beta=1 is excluded by hypothesis, as used in step 1.2.

citations.quote:
The particle and light objects of the framework are the following curves and
vector fields of the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with the physical interpretation of
[[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and the units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Worldlines] A **worldline** is a regular causal curve $x:J\to A$ in one of
the regularity classes of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] ($J$ an
order-convex subset of $\mathbb R$ with at least two elements). A **massive
worldline** is a $C^k$ future timelike worldline, $k\ge1$, with everywhere
nonzero future timelike tangent. A **future null curve** is a $C^1$ curve with
everywhere nonzero future null tangent. An **ideal vacuum light ray** of the
adopted physical model follows a null straight line: on its parameter interval
it has the form $x(s)=p+\lambda(s)v$, where $p\in A$, $v\in V$ is nonzero
future null, and $\lambda$ is $C^1$ with $\lambda'(s)>0$. This is the
straight-ray adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]]; arbitrary
future null curves are retained as kinematic objects without asserting that
they describe vacuum light propagation. Along a null curve the integrand
$-\eta(x',x')$ of the proper-time construction
([[def-sr-proper-time]]) vanishes identically, so that construction yields no
proper-time parametrization of it, and a light ray is never treated as a
massive worldline. A worldline is a curve in spacetime; its reading $r\circ x$
in a named laboratory chart is a coordinate description of it, not an object of
another observer.

(b) [Four-velocity and four-acceleration] For a massive worldline the
four-velocity $U$ and, when it is $C^2$, the four-acceleration $A$ are those of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; wherever defined they satisfy
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$, by
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(c) [Chart reading] If a massive $C^2$ worldline is described in a laboratory
chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] by $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ on an open interval of
laboratory times, then $|r'(t)|<c$ for every $t$, with four-velocity
$U=\gamma(c,r')$ and Lorentz factor
$\gamma=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, by clause (e) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(d) [Frames and observers] An inertial frame in this framework is the
origin-with-basis object of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]; a point
observer is a future unit timelike vector $n\in V$ with rest space $n^\perp$ and
rest projection $h$, as in clauses (c)-(d) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. On an open spacetime region
$W\subseteq A$, an **observer congruence field** means a $C^1$ map $n:W\to V$ with
$n(p)$ future timelike and $\eta(n(p),n(p))=-1$ at every $p$; its observer
histories, when given, are integral curves satisfying $dx/d\tau=cn(x)$.
A **tetrad field** is a tuple of $C^1$ maps $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3):W\to V^4$
whose values form a positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal basis at every
event, with $f_0$ future timelike. Regularity here means componentwise $C^1$
in inertial coordinates. These fields need not be constant and are distinct
from an inertial origin-with-basis frame, its coordinate chart and a single
point observer; no global congruence or tetrad is asserted to exist.

(e) [Scope] No force law, no self-field and no extended-body structure is
supplied here; an accelerating massive worldline requires a force model stated
separately, and an ideal light ray carries no dispersive, quantum or
polarisation structure in this definition.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where, at each original parameter $s\in J$, $\Phi=\Phi_{x(s)}$ is the
raised-index operator of the field at $x(s)$, defined by
$\eta(\Phi_{x(s)}(u),w)=F(x(s))(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to its proper-time function $\tau(s)$: explicitly
$dU/d\tau=U'(s)/\tau'(s)$, with
$\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0$. It is the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be the four-dimensional real Minkowski vector space of
[[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], with the fixed form of signature
$(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form,
$F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$
([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is
nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$
([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]],
[[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and
$\Phi:V\to V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); with
$F_{\alpha\beta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_\beta)$ in the fixed ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]] and $(\eta^{\mu\alpha})$
the inverse matrix of $(\eta_{\alpha\beta})$, one has
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, the
index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in
components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu=0$, where
$u_\mu:=\sum_\alpha\eta_{\mu\alpha}u^\alpha$ and
$F^\mu{}_\nu:=\sum_\alpha\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\nu}$. Consequently, if
$J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a
nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J\to V$ is differentiable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on
$J$ for some real $m\ne0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on
$J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). The same norm-conservation conclusion
holds for a family of skew forms $F_s$ and their pointwise operators $\Phi_s$
defined by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, when $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$: no
derivative of $F_s$ is required. In particular one may evaluate a varying field
$F_x$ along a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$. This is a conditional statement
about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any
particle.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Adopt [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]] and
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. Then the following conditional
physical claims hold in the flat classical model, with the units of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(a) Massive particle.** Let a massive particle have constant mass $m>0$,
four-momentum $P=mU$ and a future unit observer $n$. Its measured energy
$E_n(P)=-c\,\eta(P,n)$, spatial momentum $q_n(P)=h(P)$ and kinetic energy
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ satisfy $E_n(P)>0$, $T_n(P)\ge0$ and the mass-shell
identity $E_n(P)^2=m^2c^4+c^2|q_n(P)|^2$; $T_n(P)=0$ if and only if the
particle is at rest in the observer's frame ($U=cn$). In an inertial frame
whose stationary observer is $n=e_0$, the components are $P=(E/c,\mathbf p)$
with $E=E_{e_0}(P)=m\gamma_wc^2$ and $\mathbf p=m\gamma_w\mathbf w\in\mathbb R^3$
the coordinates of $q_{e_0}(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3p^ie_i$
for the coordinate velocity $\mathbf w$, and under a passive boost the
components transform as the components of the vector $P$; the combination
$E^2-c^2|\mathbf p|^2=m^2c^4$ is frame-independent.

**(b) Four-force.** Along a $C^2$ worldline with four-acceleration $A$, the
four-force $F=\dot P$ satisfies $\eta(P,F)=0$ and $F=mA$; in an inertial frame
$F=\gamma\,(\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w/c,\ \mathbf f)$ and
$dE/dt=\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w$, where $\mathbf f=d\mathbf p/dt$ is the
coordinate three-force. The constancy of $m$ is used; if instead $m$ is a
$C^1$ function $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ along the same worldline, define $P:=mU$
and $F:=\dot P$ by the general derivative construction. As a mathematical identity, $\eta(P,F)=-mc^2\,dm/d\tau$, and the
constant-mass identities are not transferred to variable-mass systems.

**(c) System mass.** For a finite nonempty system of particles all of whose
four-momenta are nonzero future causal, let $Q:=\sum_iP_i$. If $Q$ is
future timelike, its invariant mass $M=\sqrt{-\eta(Q,Q)}/c$ satisfies: in the
center-of-momentum frame with $e_0=Q/(Mc)$ one has
$Mc^2=\sum_iE_{e_0}(P_i)$; every massive constituent has
$E_{e_0}(P_i)\ge m_ic^2$, with equality exactly when it is at rest in that
frame, and every massless constituent has $E_{e_0}(P_i)>0$. Hence
$M\ge\sum_im_i$ over the massive constituents, with equality if and only if
the system is massive-only and all its constituents are at rest in the
center-of-momentum frame. If $Q$ is future null, then $M=0$, all constituents
are massless with parallel momenta, and no center-of-momentum frame exists.

**(d) Massless particle.** An ideal massless particle has
$E_n(P)=c\,|q_n(P)|>0$, has no rest frame and is not $mU$ for any $m>0$; it is
not obtained from the massive formula by setting $m=0$.

**(e) Necessary collision thresholds.** Suppose that, under the adopted
isolated-collision balance, an isolated collision occurs whose incoming legs
are massive particles of constant masses $m_1,\dots,m_N$ and whose outgoing
legs are massive particles of masses $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_K$ and possibly ideal
massless particles. Let $M$ be the invariant mass of the common total
four-momentum $Q$. Then the necessary inequalities $M\ge\sum_im_i$ and
$M\ge\sum_j\mu_j$ hold; if the incoming side is a projectile of mass $m_1$
and a target of mass $m_2$ at rest in the observer frame of the target, with
projectile energy $E$ and kinetic energy $T=E-m_1c^2$ in that frame, then

$$E\ \ge\ \frac{c^2}{2m_2}\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K\mu_j\Bigr)^2-m_1^2-m_2^2\Bigr],\qquad T\ \ge\ \frac{c^2}{2m_2}\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K\mu_j\Bigr)^2-(m_1+m_2)^2\Bigr],$$

Separately, under the same adopted balance, a single incoming massless particle
cannot produce an outgoing state containing a massive particle. These are kinematic necessity statements under
the adopted conservation: they do not assert that any collision occurs, do
not fix probabilities, amplitudes or cross sections, and are not empirical
findings.

**(f) Scope.** All clauses are conditional on the two postulates and on the
stated idealisations; the conclusions carry the same idealisations. No
measurement, precision, statistical or empirical claim is made.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the relativistic particle model, on top of the
flat spacetime model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and the SI unit
conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], together with
the framework's idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks and ideal light
signals:

**(i) Mass and momentum.** Every massive classical particle of the model
carries a positive constant invariant mass parameter $m>0$ and has
four-momentum $P=mU$, where $U$ is the four-velocity of its future timelike
worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]],
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]); $P$ is a vector of $V$
whose SI unit is kilogram metre per second. The formula is adopted only for
$m>0$; the case $m=0$ is not defined by it and is the separate premise
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. In particular $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$
is a consequence of the four-velocity normalisation, not a separate
assumption.

**(ii) Observer measurement identification.** Relative to a future unit
observer $n$, the model identifies the measured energy of the particle with
$E_n(P)$, its measured spatial momentum with $q_n(P)$, its kinetic energy with
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ and its rest energy with $mc^2$, where $E_n,q_n,T_n$ are
the quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; the
units are the joule, kilogram metre per second and kilogram of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. This clause is a formulation
convention identifying mathematical quantities with the quantities the model
calls measured; it is not a measurement report and no experiment is claimed.

**(iii) Isolated collision balance.** An isolated collision is represented by
a mass-specified on-shell collision datum at an event, with finite nonempty
incoming and outgoing lists of the massive particles of (i) and/or the ideal
massless particles of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]], and with
no external four-momentum transfer or omitted leg. The interaction is
idealized as confined to that event. The sum of the incoming four-momenta equals the sum of the
outgoing four-momenta, in the sense of the collision data of
[[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: the model adopts
$Q_{\mathrm{in}}=Q_{\mathrm{out}}$ for such an isolated datum. No particular
collision is asserted to occur, and no mechanism, probability, cross section
or amplitude is supplied by this clause.

**(iv) Equation of motion for a stipulated force.** Put
$H_c^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. A stipulated force law is a given
map $F:D\to V$ on a given subset $D\subseteq A\times H_c^+$,
with force components in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$. No regularity
away from the specified worldline is assumed. Along a given $C^2$ massive worldline
$x:I\to A$ with $(x(s),U(s))\in D$ for all $s\in I$, the model's particle
equation is $m\,dU/d\tau=F(x,U)$, with
$dU/d\tau$ the proper-time derivative of
[[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]], so that the stipulated $F$
is the four-force of the motion. A particular force law, and the existence,
uniqueness and domain of solutions of the resulting equation, are not adopted
here and belong to a separate model.

Empirical support for these assumptions is a nonlogical relation of the
framework, not a proof; the idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks,
ideal light signals and flat spacetime are inherited and travel to every
consumer of this premise.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $(V,\eta)$ be the four-dimensional real Minkowski vector space of
[[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], with the fixed form of signature
$(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form,
$F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$
([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is
nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$
([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]],
[[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and
$\Phi:V\to V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); with
$F_{\alpha\beta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_\beta)$ in the fixed ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]] and $(\eta^{\mu\alpha})$
the inverse matrix of $(\eta_{\alpha\beta})$, one has
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, the
index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in
components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu=0$, where
$u_\mu:=\sum_\alpha\eta_{\mu\alpha}u^\alpha$ and
$F^\mu{}_\nu:=\sum_\alpha\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\nu}$. Consequently, if
$J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a
nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J\to V$ is differentiable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on
$J$ for some real $m\ne0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on
$J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). The same norm-conservation conclusion
holds for a family of skew forms $F_s$ and their pointwise operators $\Phi_s$
defined by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, when $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$: no
derivative of $F_s$ is required. In particular one may evaluate a varying field
$F_x$ along a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$. This is a conditional statement
about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any
particle.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.
If $a>0$ and $r\in\mathbb Q$, then the real power $a^r=\exp(r\log a)$ agrees with the rational power of [[def-rational-power]]. For $r>0$, both conventions also give $0^r=0$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r < s$
([[def-rat-order]]), with rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]].

1. **In the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^{r} < a^{s}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^{r} = a^{s} = 1$; if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^{r} > a^{s}$.
2. **In the base.** If $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r > 0$ and $0 < a < b$, then $a^{r} < b^{r}$; so $a \mapsto a^{r}$ is strictly increasing on $\{a \in \mathbb{R} : a > 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with $1$.** For rational $t > 0$: $a > 1$ implies $a^{t} > 1$, and $0 < a < 1$ implies $a^{t} < 1$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as functions on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)\,g'(c) \;=\; \bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr)\,f'(c) .$$

**The statement is a product identity, and that is deliberate.** The familiar
quotient form

$$\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)} \;=\; \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}$$

is not asserted here, and it is not equivalent: its left side needs
$g(b) \ne g(a)$ and its right side needs $g'(c) \ne 0$, and neither follows from
the hypotheses. The product form above needs neither, holds under exactly the
hypotheses stated, and specialises to the quotient form whenever both
denominators happen to be nonzero. The companion page exhibits an $f$ and a $g$
for which the quotient form is meaningless while the product form holds.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: (Clause (a): the coordinate force) By [F1] and [F5], $U=\gamma(c,v)$, $U^i=\gamma v_i$ and $\mathrm d/\mathrm d\tau=\gamma\,\mathrm d/\mathrm dt$ (chain rule for the inverse parametrization $t\mapsto\tau(t)$), and $p=m\gamma v$ by [F4]. For a spatial index $i$, the spatial component of the equation of motion [F2] reads $m\,dU^i/d\tau=q\,\Phi(U)^i=q\gamma\bigl(E_i+(v\times B)_i\bigr)$ by [F3]. Since $U^i=\gamma v_i$ and $p_i=m\gamma v_i$, the left side is $m\,dU^i/d\tau=m\gamma\,\frac{d}{dt}(\gamma v_i)=\gamma\,\frac{dp_i}{dt}$, so $\gamma\,dp_i/dt=q\gamma(E_i+(v\times B)_i)$ and, dividing by $\gamma>0$, $dp_i/dt=q(E_i+(v\times B)_i)$ for $i=1,2,3$; componentwise this is $dp/dt=q(E+v\times B)$. The derivatives are those of the chart time, and $E,B$ are the laboratory components of $F$.

(Clause (a): the power identity) For the temporal index, [F2] and [F3] give $m\,dU^0/d\tau=q\,\Phi(U)^0=q\gamma E\cdot v/c$. By [F1] and [F5], $U^0=\gamma c$ and $dU^0/d\tau=\gamma c\,\mathrm d\gamma/\mathrm dt$, so $m\,dU^0/d\tau=\frac{\gamma}{c}\,mc^2\frac{\mathrm d\gamma}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\gamma}{c}\frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}$; comparing with the right-hand side, $\frac{\gamma}{c}\frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}=\frac{q\gamma E\cdot v}{c}$, and multiplying by $c/\gamma>0$ gives $d(\gamma mc^2)/dt=q\,E\cdot v$.

(Clause (b): norm preservation and the future branch) At every interior parameter $s\in J$, the proper-time derivative in [F2] is $dU/d\tau=U'(s)/\tau'(s)$, with $\tau'(s)>0$. Thus $U'(s)=(q/m)\tau'(s)\Phi_{x(s)}(U(s))$. The product rule and pointwise skew orthogonality [F6] give $\frac{d}{ds}\eta(U,U)=2\eta(U,U')=2(q/m)\tau'(s)\eta(U,\Phi_{x(s)}(U))=0$; no derivative of the field is used. The scalar $\eta(U,U)$ is continuous on $J$; the mean value theorem [F8] on every compact subinterval therefore makes it constant, including any included endpoints. Its value is $-c^2$ by [F1]. Consequently $(U^0)^2=c^2+|U_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2>0$, so $U^0$ never vanishes. Continuity and the intermediate value theorem [F6] show that its sign is constant on $J$; if $U^0(s_0)>0$ at any initial parameter $s_0\in J$, then $U^0>0$ throughout. The solution remains future timelike and $|v(t)|<c$ wherever its chart reading is differentiable, by [F1]. No existence or continuation of solutions is asserted.

(Clause (c): the function and its derivatives) Put $z(t):=|v(t)|^2/c^2$, so that $0\le z\le\delta^2$ on an interval where $|v|/c\le\delta$, $\delta\in(0,1)$, and $\gamma=f(z)$ with $f(z):=(1-z)^{-1/2}$. The function $f$ is continuous on $[0,\delta^2]$ and differentiable on $(0,\delta^2)$: it is the composition of $z\mapsto1-z$ with $y\mapsto y^{-1/2}$, the latter continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ with derivative $-\tfrac12y^{-3/2}$ [F7], and $\gamma=f(z)$ agrees with the rational power of [F1] by [F7]. By the chain rule [F5], $f'(z)=\tfrac12(1-z)^{-3/2}$ and $f''(z)=\tfrac34(1-z)^{-5/2}$ on $(0,\delta^2)$. If $z=0$ then $\gamma=1$ and every difference and bound in clause (c) vanishes exactly; hence assume $0<z\le\delta^2$ below, and note $1-\delta^2>0$.

(Clause (c): first-order bound) Since $f$ is continuous on $[0,z]$ and differentiable on $(0,z)$, [F8] gives $\xi\in(0,z)$ with $f(z)-f(0)=f'(\xi)z$, and $f(0)=1$; hence $|\gamma-1|=|f'(\xi)|\,z=\tfrac12(1-\xi)^{-3/2}z$. Since $0<\xi\le z\le\delta^2<1$, the base satisfies $1-\xi\ge1-\delta^2>0$, so $0<(1-\xi)^{-3/2}\le(1-\delta^2)^{-3/2}$ by monotonicity of the positive power and positivity of inverses [F7]; therefore $|\gamma-1|\le\frac{z}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{|v|^2/c^2}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}$.

(Clause (c): second-order bound) Define $q(s):=f(s)-1-\tfrac{s}{2}$ and $g(s):=s^2$ on $[0,z]$; both are continuous on $[0,z]$ and differentiable on $(0,z)$, with $q'(s)=f'(s)-\tfrac12$ and $g'(s)=2s>0$ there [F7, F8]. Cauchy's mean value theorem [F8] gives $\xi\in(0,z)$ with $\bigl(q(z)-q(0)\bigr)g'(\xi)=\bigl(g(z)-g(0)\bigr)q'(\xi)$; since $q(0)=0=g(0)$, $g'(\xi)=2\xi\ne0$ and $q'(\xi)=f'(\xi)-\tfrac12$, this reads $f(z)-1-\tfrac z2=\frac{z^2}{2\xi}\bigl(f'(\xi)-\tfrac12\bigr)$. The mean value theorem [F8] applied to $f'$ on $[0,\xi]$, where $f'$ is continuous on $[0,\xi]$ and differentiable on $(0,\xi)$ (the derivative $f''$ is given on $(0,\delta^2)$ in step 1.4), gives $\eta\in(0,\xi)$ with $f'(\xi)-f'(0)=\xi f''(\eta)$; since $f'(0)=\tfrac12$ this gives $f'(\xi)-\tfrac12=\xi f''(\eta)$, and substitution yields $f(z)-1-\tfrac z2=\frac{z^2}{2\xi}\cdot\xi f''(\eta)=\tfrac12f''(\eta)z^2=\tfrac38(1-\eta)^{-5/2}z^2$. Since $0<\eta\le\xi\le z\le\delta^2$, monotonicity of the positive power [F7] gives $(1-\eta)^{-5/2}\le(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}$, hence $\bigl|\gamma-1-\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2}\bigr|=\bigl|f(z)-1-\tfrac z2\bigr|\le\frac38(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}z^2=\frac38(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}\bigl(\frac{|v|^2}{c^2}\bigr)^2$.

(Clause (c): the momentum and energy bounds) Multiplying the first-order bound of step 2.1 by $m|v|\ge0$ and using $|xy|=|x||y|$ [F8] gives $|p-mv|=|m\gamma v-mv|=m|v|\,|\gamma-1|\le m|v|\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}$. Multiplying the second-order bound of step 2.2 by $mc^2>0$ gives $\bigl|\gamma mc^2-mc^2-\tfrac12m|v|^2\bigr|=mc^2\bigl|\gamma-1-\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2}\bigr|\le\frac38(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}\frac{m|v|^4}{c^2}$. The constants depend only on $\delta$, so both bounds are uniform on any interval where $|v|/c\le\delta$. These are pointwise algebraic bounds; no approximation of the trajectory over a time interval is asserted.

(Clauses (c) and (d): status and scope) Clauses (a) and (b) are steps 1.1-1.3, and clause (c) is steps 1.4, 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1: the two first-order and second-order bounds, the resulting momentum and energy bounds and their uniformity in $|v|/c\le\delta$ are established there, including the exact vanishing at $z=0$. The charge $q$ is a constant parameter of [[def-em-sources]] (a), $m>0$ is an externally supplied rest mass, and $F$ is a prescribed exterior field $C^1$ near the graph: the particle's own field, radiation reaction and any self-force are excluded, as are magnetic monopoles and zero or variable mass [F2]. The nonrelativistic coordinate law is not adopted as exact; clause (c) is a controlled kinematic expansion and asserts no trajectory approximation over time, which would require a separate stability argument. The argument used the metric contraction [F3], the coupling [F2], the momentum and four-force identification [F4], the proper-time chain rule [F5], the orthogonality and norm-conservation lemma [F6] (whose varying-field clause was used so that no derivative of $F$ enters), and the power and mean value tools [F7], [F8]; it is conditional on the adopted postulates, makes no empirical claim and uses no choice principle.

boundaries.reason: The statement concerns one worldline with fixed parameters on an interval; no finite set, family, sequence or union is quantified over.

boundaries.evidence: The rest case z=|v|^2/c^2=0 is exact in step 1.4: gamma=1 and every difference and bound in clause (c) vanishes exactly; steps 2.1 and 2.2 then state their bounds under the separately noted assumption 0<z<=delta^2.

boundaries.reason: No one-element family, unit vector construction or singleton index set occurs; the four-velocity, charge and mass are the general fixed objects.

boundaries.evidence: The bounded-speed regime has delta in (0,1): the degenerate limit delta->1 is excluded by 1-delta^2>0 used in step 1.4 and by the positive lower bounds 1-xi>=1-delta^2>0 and 1-eta>=1-delta^2>0 in steps 2.1 and 2.2.

Steps 2.1 and 2.2 apply the mean value and Cauchy mean value theorems on the closed interval [0,z] including both endpoints (continuity on [0,z], differentiability on (0,z)) and step 1.4 disposes of the endpoint z=0 exactly; step 3.1 gives constants uniform in |v|/c<=delta.

boundaries.reason: The constants delta, m and q are fixed parameters and the expansions are computed deterministically; step 4.1 records that no choice principle is used.
Clauses (a)-(d) are identities, a conservation statement and two-sided bounds; the item asserts no biconditional statement, so no forward iff case arises.
No converse of an iff claim is asserted; in particular clause (c) is an explicitly one-sided controlled expansion with no trajectory approximation claimed, as step 4.1 states.
