citations.quote:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

The particle and light objects of the framework are the following curves and
vector fields of the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with the physical interpretation of
[[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and the units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Worldlines] A **worldline** is a regular causal curve $x:J\to A$ in one of
the regularity classes of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] ($J$ an
order-convex subset of $\mathbb R$ with at least two elements). A **massive
worldline** is a $C^k$ future timelike worldline, $k\ge1$, with everywhere
nonzero future timelike tangent. A **future null curve** is a $C^1$ curve with
everywhere nonzero future null tangent. An **ideal vacuum light ray** of the
adopted physical model follows a null straight line: on its parameter interval
it has the form $x(s)=p+\lambda(s)v$, where $p\in A$, $v\in V$ is nonzero
future null, and $\lambda$ is $C^1$ with $\lambda'(s)>0$. This is the
straight-ray adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]]; arbitrary
future null curves are retained as kinematic objects without asserting that
they describe vacuum light propagation. Along a null curve the integrand
$-\eta(x',x')$ of the proper-time construction
([[def-sr-proper-time]]) vanishes identically, so that construction yields no
proper-time parametrization of it, and a light ray is never treated as a
massive worldline. A worldline is a curve in spacetime; its reading $r\circ x$
in a named laboratory chart is a coordinate description of it, not an object of
another observer.

(b) [Four-velocity and four-acceleration] For a massive worldline the
four-velocity $U$ and, when it is $C^2$, the four-acceleration $A$ are those of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; wherever defined they satisfy
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$, by
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(c) [Chart reading] If a massive $C^2$ worldline is described in a laboratory
chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] by $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ on an open interval of
laboratory times, then $|r'(t)|<c$ for every $t$, with four-velocity
$U=\gamma(c,r')$ and Lorentz factor
$\gamma=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, by clause (e) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(d) [Frames and observers] An inertial frame in this framework is the
origin-with-basis object of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]; a point
observer is a future unit timelike vector $n\in V$ with rest space $n^\perp$ and
rest projection $h$, as in clauses (c)-(d) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. On an open spacetime region
$W\subseteq A$, an **observer congruence field** means a $C^1$ map $n:W\to V$ with
$n(p)$ future timelike and $\eta(n(p),n(p))=-1$ at every $p$; its observer
histories, when given, are integral curves satisfying $dx/d\tau=cn(x)$.
A **tetrad field** is a tuple of $C^1$ maps $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3):W\to V^4$
whose values form a positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal basis at every
event, with $f_0$ future timelike. Regularity here means componentwise $C^1$
in inertial coordinates. These fields need not be constant and are distinct
from an inertial origin-with-basis frame, its coordinate chart and a single
point observer; no global congruence or tetrad is asserted to exist.

(e) [Scope] No force law, no self-field and no extended-body structure is
supplied here; an accelerating massive worldline requires a force model stated
separately, and an ideal light ray carries no dispersive, quantum or
polarisation structure in this definition.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Assume the framework's spacetime, field and worldline objects of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]], with the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and clause (i) of the adopted Lorentz coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]: a constant charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-sources]] (a), an externally supplied rest mass $m>0$, a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline $x:J\to A$ with four-velocity $U$, and a prescribed field $F$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle; the adopted equation of motion is $$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),\qquad \eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u),$$ $U$ the four-velocity of [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] (b) with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$. Let $t\mapsto r(t)$ be the laboratory chart reading of the worldline, $v:=r'$ its coordinate velocity and $\gamma:=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, so that $U=\gamma(c,v)$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] (e)). Then, wherever the worldline is $C^2$: (a) [Coordinate force and power] with the coordinate three-momentum $p:=m\gamma v$ of [[pthm-sr-momentum-and-four-force]] (a), $$\frac{dp}{dt}=q\,(E+v\times B),\qquad \frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}=q\,E\cdot v,$$ the derivatives taken with respect to the chart time $t$ and $E,B$ the components of $F$ in the laboratory frame. (b) [Norm preservation] $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$ with value $-c^2$; in particular a solution with future timelike initial data remains future timelike, and $|v(t)|<c$ wherever the reading is differentiable ([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]). (c) [Controlled low-speed expansion] for every $\delta\in(0,1)$, on any interval where $|v|/c\le\delta$, $$|\gamma-1|\le\frac{|v|^2/c^2}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad \Bigl|\gamma-1-\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2}\Bigr|\le\frac{3}{8}(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}\Bigl(\frac{|v|^2}{c^2}\Bigr)^{2},$$ and consequently $$|p-mv|\le m|v|\,\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad \Bigl|\gamma mc^2-mc^2-\tfrac12m|v|^2\Bigr|\le\frac{3}{8}(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}\frac{m|v|^4}{c^2};$$ the constants depend only on $\delta$, so the bounds are uniform in $|v|/c\le\delta$. These are pointwise algebraic expansions; they assert no approximation of the trajectory over a time interval, which would require a separate stability argument. (d) [Scope] The charge is constant, $m>0$ is an externally supplied parameter and $F$ is a prescribed exterior field: the particle's own field, radiation reaction and any self-force are excluded, as are magnetic monopoles and zero or variable mass; the nonrelativistic coordinate law is not adopted as exact, and (c) is a controlled kinematic expansion, not a trajectory approximation. The statement is conditional on the adopted postulates and makes no empirical claim.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be the four-dimensional real Minkowski vector space of
[[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], with the fixed form of signature
$(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form,
$F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$
([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is
nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$
([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]],
[[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and
$\Phi:V\to V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); with
$F_{\alpha\beta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_\beta)$ in the fixed ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]] and $(\eta^{\mu\alpha})$
the inverse matrix of $(\eta_{\alpha\beta})$, one has
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, the
index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in
components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu=0$, where
$u_\mu:=\sum_\alpha\eta_{\mu\alpha}u^\alpha$ and
$F^\mu{}_\nu:=\sum_\alpha\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\nu}$. Consequently, if
$J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a
nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J\to V$ is differentiable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on
$J$ for some real $m\ne0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on
$J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). The same norm-conservation conclusion
holds for a family of skew forms $F_s$ and their pointwise operators $\Phi_s$
defined by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, when $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$: no
derivative of $F_s$ is required. In particular one may evaluate a varying field
$F_x$ along a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$. This is a conditional statement
about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any
particle.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$
If $a>0$ and $r\in\mathbb Q$, then the real power $a^r=\exp(r\log a)$ agrees with the rational power of [[def-rational-power]]. For $r>0$, both conventions also give $0^r=0$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

derivations.claim: The prescribed field is source-free: $E\equiv E_0e_1$ and $B\equiv0$ are constant, so every first partial derivative of every component vanishes; by the component formulas of [F2], $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{curl}B=0$ and $\partial_tE=\partial_tB=0$, so the four source-free smooth-branch equations hold on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

The trajectory and its velocity ($h\ne0$): put $g(t):=\sqrt{1+h^2t^2}=(1+h^2t^2)^{1/2}$, a composition of the positive polynomial $t\mapsto1+h^2t^2$ with the power $x\mapsto x^{1/2}$; by [F4] and the chain rule [F5], $g$ is differentiable with $g'(t)=\tfrac12(1+h^2t^2)^{-1/2}\cdot2h^2t=h^2t/g(t)$, and since every derivative is a rational expression with nonzero denominator $g$, iterating the same rules shows $g$ and hence $r(t)=r_0+\tfrac{c}{h}(g(t)-1)e_1$ are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$. Then $r'(t)=\tfrac{c}{h}g'(t)e_1=\tfrac{c ht}{g(t)}e_1=v(t)$ by [F5], so $|v(t)|=c|ht|/g(t)<c$ because $h^2t^2<1+h^2t^2$ for all real $t$ [F5], and $|v(t)|\to c$ as $|t|\to\infty$ because $|ht|/g(t)\to1$.

The branch $h=0$: here $q=0$ since $E_0>0$, $m>0$ and $h=qE_0/(mc)$; the definition gives $r\equiv r_0$, $v\equiv0$, $\gamma\equiv1$ and $p\equiv0$, so $dp/dt=0=q(E+v\times B)$ and $d(\gamma mc^2)/dt=0=qE\cdot v$ hold trivially, and the Newtonian comparison trajectory of clause (iii) is $r_N\equiv r_0$ as well, with $v_N\equiv0$; the formulas containing $1/h$ are not used in this branch.

Force and power identities ($h\ne0$): by step 1.2, $\gamma(t)=g(t)$ equals $(1-|v(t)|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, since $1-|v|^2/c^2=1-\frac{h^2t^2}{1+h^2t^2}=\frac{1}{g(t)^2}$; hence $p(t)=m\gamma(t)v(t)=mg(t)\cdot\frac{c ht}{g(t)}e_1=mch t\,e_1=qE_0t\,e_1$, because $mch=qE_0$. Therefore $dp/dt=qE_0e_1=q(E+v\times B)$, since $E=E_0e_1$, $B=0$ and $v\times0=0$ [F5]. For the power identity, $d(\gamma mc^2)/dt=mc^2g'(t)=mc^2h^2t/g(t)=qE_0\cdot v_1(t)$ because $qE_0=mch$ and $v_1(t)=cht/g(t)$. These are the two coordinate identities of [F3]. The covariant equation $m\,dU/d\tau=q\Phi(U)$ of [F3] also holds: with $U^0=g(t)c$, $U^1=cht$ and $U^2=U^3=0$ one has $dU^0/d\tau=g\,d(gc)/dt=c\,g\,g'=ch^2t$ and $dU^1/d\tau=g\,d(cht)/dt=cgh$, so $m\,dU^0/d\tau=mch^2t=qE_0ht=q\Phi(U)^0$ and $m\,dU^1/d\tau=mgch=qgE_0=q\Phi(U)^1$, while the components $2,3$ vanish on both sides; hence the displayed curve is an exact solution of the adopted coupling in this special model.

The curve is a future timelike worldline: by step 1.2 the curve is $C^\infty$ with coordinate velocity $v(t)$ and $|v(t)|<c$; its tangent $(c,v(t))$ has $\eta$-square $-c^2+|v(t)|^2<0$ and positive time component $c>0$, so it is future timelike at every $t$, and the chart reading is that of a massive worldline in the sense of [F1]. At $h=0$ the constant curve has tangent $(c,0)$, also future timelike.

The unscoped Newtonian extrapolation ($h\ne0$): define $v_N(t):=(qE_0/m)t\,e_1=hct\,e_1$ and $r_N(t):=r_0+\tfrac12hct^2e_1$. Since $qE_0/m=hc$, step 1.2 gives $v(t)=\frac{cht}{g(t)}e_1=\frac{v_N(t)}{g(t)}=\frac{v_N(t)}{\sqrt{1+h^2t^2}}$, and therefore $|v_N(t)|=g(t)|v(t)|=c|ht|$, which exceeds $c$ exactly when $|ht|>1$, while $|v(t)|<c$ for every finite $t$ by step 1.2. The two velocities agree only at $t=0$; $v_N$ is the Newtonian constant-acceleration prediction of the unscoped law.

Error bounds ($h\ne0$): put $s:=ht$ and $g=\sqrt{1+s^2}\ge1$. Rationalisation gives $g-1=\frac{s^2}{g+1}\le\frac{s^2}{2}$ and $1-\frac1g=\frac{g-1}{g}\le\frac{s^2}{2}$; hence $|v-v_N|=|v_N|\bigl|1-\frac1g\bigr|=c|s|\bigl(1-\frac1g\bigr)\le\frac{c}{2}|s|^3$, which is the velocity bound. For the displacement, $r(t)-r_N(t)=\frac{c}{h}\bigl(g-1-\tfrac{s^2}{2}\bigr)e_1$, and the elementary identity $1+\tfrac{s^2}{2}-g=\tfrac{(g-1)^2}{2}$ gives $\bigl|g-1-\tfrac{s^2}{2}\bigr|=\tfrac{(g-1)^2}{2}\le\tfrac{s^4}{8}$ by the first inequality; multiplying by $c/|h|$ gives $|r-r_N|\le\frac{c}{8|h|}|s|^4$. Consequently on $|ht|\le\delta$ the velocity error is at most $c\delta^3/2$ and the displacement error at most $c\delta^4/(8|h|)$; these are special-model comparisons for this explicit solution and do not import a general trajectory-stability consequence of [[pthm-em-relativistic-lorentz-force]] (c).

Closing and scope: the prescribed field is a source-free constant smooth-branch solution (step 1.1); for $h\ne0$ the displayed curve is $C^\infty$, future timelike and subluminal at every finite time, and it satisfies the force and power identities with $p=qE_0te_1$ (steps 1.2, 2.1, 2.2); the Newtonian comparison and its exact superluminal condition are step 2.3, and the special-model error bounds are step 3.1; the branch $h=0$ with $q=0$ is step 1.3. The field is prescribed and external, the particle's own field, radiation reaction and any self-force are excluded, no production of the field is described, and no measurement or empirical claim is made. The argument used the field and worldline objects [F1], the smooth-branch equations [F2], the force and power identities [F3], the power and root calculus [F4] and the chain and product rules [F5]; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The example explicitly defines E,B on R^3 x R and r:R -> R^3; it fixes one field pair, one particle and one trajectory, with no empty-family case.

boundaries.evidence: The h=0 branch (equivalently q=0) is treated separately in step 1.3: r identically r_0, v identically 0, gamma identically 1, both force and power identities hold trivially, the 1/h formulas are not used, and step 2.2 confirms the constant curve is future timelike.

boundaries.reason: No unit case or one-element family occurs; the parameters q, E_0, m, r_0 and h are the general fixed data of the example.

boundaries.evidence: The degenerate parameter h=0 is separated in steps 1.3 and 2.2 where gamma=1 and the 1/h limits are excluded, and the comparison degeneracy |v_N|>c exactly when |ht|>1 is identified in step 2.3 while the exact solution stays subluminal at every finite t by step 1.2. Supplemental retained check (formerly square-comparison-signs): F5 requires both a,b>=0 as in lem-of-square-monotone. In step 1.2 compare |ht| and sqrt(1+h²t²), both nonnegative; in step 3.1 g>=1 and g-1>=0 justify squared comparisons. The excluded b<0 counterexample a=1,b=-2 invalidated the former fact.

For h!=0, step 1.2 gives |v(t)|<c at every finite t and |v(t)|->c at both infinities; for h=0 the speed is identically zero (step 1.3). Step 3.1 bounds are uniform on |ht|<=delta, including endpoints, and use h!=0 for the displacement denominator.

boundaries.reason: All functions are explicit in the parameters q, E_0, m and r_0; the closing step 4.1 records that no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.3 establishes |v_N(t)|=c|ht| and hence the forward implication |ht|>1 => |v_N(t)|>c, the Newtonian comparison becoming superluminal, exactly as stated.

The reverse implication |v_N(t)|<=c for |ht|<=1 is the same evaluation |v_N(t)|=c|ht| of step 2.3, which also notes the velocities agree only at t=0, disposing of the converse of the exactly-when claim.
